operator_plays.name: Reserved Bare-Metal H100/H200 Cluster Slicing & Multi-Provider Inference Router Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Commit to wholesale bare-metal or reserved H100/H200/B200 GPU capacity where resale is permitted, then serve isolated multi-tenant quantized vLLM inference and interruptible batch queues through a multi-provider router. Separately resell authorized wholesale SIP and registered 10DLC capacity. Target a 35%–55% net spread after upstream and operating costs; utilization, hardware depreciation, quality requirements and carrier pricing can erase that spread.
inputs: Resale-permitted GPU reservations and approved wholesale telecom agreements with explicit capacity, SLA and acceptable-use terms
Tenant-isolated vLLM inference and provider routing with quantization validation, DCGM metering and protected customer data
Prepaid usage billing, demand commitments and role-appropriate KYC, telecom registration and abuse-response controls
workflow: 1. Validate committed customer demand, benchmark models and negotiate resale-permitted GPU and telecom capacity against conservative utilization forecasts.
2. Configure isolated workloads, licensed models, retention controls and usage metering; establish required telecom registrations and consent controls before activation.
3. Route authorized inference and batch jobs by quality, latency and landed cost while provisioning only vetted, compliant SIP and 10DLC traffic.
4. Reconcile prepaid usage against provider bills, rebalance or reduce commitments when permitted and suspend abusive tenants under documented procedures.
metrics: Net contribution percentage after GPU commitments, carrier costs, bandwidth, support and payment expenses
Billable GPU utilization and inference cost per million tokens at the required quality and latency
Prepaid balance coverage, tenant isolation incidents and telecom abuse complaint rate

platform_risks.failure_mode: Committed capacity remains underused or abusive traffic causes upstream suspension
platform_risks.trigger: Demand shortfall, rapid market price compression, tenant isolation failure or prohibited compute or calling activity
platform_risks.impact: Negative margin, stranded commitments, customer service interruption and regulatory exposure
platform_risks.detection_metric: Utilization below break-even, prepaid balance deficits, isolation alerts and carrier abuse notices
platform_risks.fallback: Suspend abusive workloads, preserve required evidence, route compliant traffic only to authorized alternatives and reduce or renegotiate excess commitments

chapters.question_prompt: How do practitioners hand-build, host, and monetize their own GPU rental rigs, and what carries over from (and goes wrong in) GPU crypto mining?
chapters.title: From Mining Rig to AI Rental Rig: Building and Hosting Your Own GPUs for Profit
chapters.subtitle: Hand-building 100 to 1,000 GPU servers, CMP 170HX and budget 'AI' card rental servers, $3,000 rental-PC payback math, $10K of rental-platform testing, Nvidia's home mini-datacenter payouts, CLORE and Pearl/Monero dual mining, rig power and cooling math, FPGA competition, Windows interrupt crashes, and cryptojacking malware
chapters.executive_summary: Operators who moved from crypto mining to AI rentals agree the money now sits in renting VRAM, not hashing. Red Panda Mining calls GPU mining dead at residential power, while Modern Mining and BearMarketMiner report daily rental income from 4090, 5090 and 4060 Ti rigs. The shared prerequisites are fiber or strong symmetric upload, high system RAM, NVMe storage, and power infrastructure held near 80% load. The street numbers: Vast takes about 25%, SimplePod 20%, and Salad 10% plus 40 cents. A 4090 on Salad nets about $2.92 a day, a 10x 170HX server pulled $36.37 in a day, and Alec Glover's chassis run $1,500-$2,000. The disagreements are newest-generation hardware versus cheap PCIe 3.0 servers, building versus buying with a warranty, and high-end versus budget cards.

sections.heading: 1. The Practitioner Consensus: Rented VRAM Replaced Hashrate
paragraphs: The operators who lived through the Ethereum era agree the hashing business is finished and rented VRAM is the replacement. Red Panda Mining puts it without hedging: 'GPU mining is dead, and it's not profitable at all, especially at any residential electric.' The same operator has redirected cards, servers and traded-in ASICs into rental fleets [mfQE_CptyLA @ 00:04:26]. Modern Mining reaches the same conclusion from a single-card consumer build. A long parts-and-profit walkthrough ends with 'Do not buy crypto miners,' and the channel runs eight rigs on rental software instead [WJnsgbZsg0U @ 00:42:42]. Mining-native channels quietly concede the point. Honey With Crypto frames a 5 to 6 lakh rupee rig as dead capital if its coin collapses and names AI GPU renting as the escape hatch [Wp6L77ZvZw8 @ 00:00:22]. Crypto Miners Rigs, running about 50 miners, adds a hard rule: if revenue minus power doesn't leave a cushion, don't buy the cards for mining alone. The channel also notes that GPUs, unlike ASICs, keep their resale value [1q_WZwOjByQ @ 00:07:22]. That resale angle is what makes the pivot workable. Silicon that stopped paying on hashrate can be relisted to renters who pay by the hour for memory and compute.

The second point of agreement is that renters pick machines on infrastructure, not just on the GPU model. Red Panda Mining runs its rental boxes on fiber internet with a static IP and reports Vast machines getting verified within one to two days on that setup. The channel is also fitting a 4 TB Samsung NVMe to the V100 server [ET1JYocpu0M @ 00:08:32]. Modern Mining sets the connectivity floor at 500 Mb, runs eight rigs on a 1 Gb symmetric line, and stresses that upload is the number that matters [WJnsgbZsg0U @ 00:10:01]. BearMarketMiner measured the memory effect directly on OctaSpace. A 26 GB rig landed 7 rentals in roughly 30 days, while a 63 GB rig landed 82. Both test builds carried 64 GB of system RAM, paired with a 1 TB disk and at least 100/100 internet as the OctaSpace baseline [egH5hKD913Y @ 00:10:53]. At warehouse scale Alec Glover applies the same thinking to storage. Every node gets four U.2 drives through an SFF-8654 backplane, treated as scratch space or RAID0 rather than primary storage [CgsDEFaGLJ0 @ 00:18:33]. The shared lesson is that a fast card stuck behind thin RAM, slow disks or weak upload simply sits unrented.

Power discipline is the third shared baseline, and the mining and data-center camps use the same number. Alec Glover runs all power infrastructure at a consistent 80% steady-state load. A 4090 server is sized at about 4.6 kW (GPU TDP plus 1,000 W) on four 1,600 W supplies, and 5090 servers move to five supplies with one PDU each [CgsDEFaGLJ0 @ 00:27:42]. Crypto Miners Rigs applies the same 80% rule to an open-frame rig. Count cards at their planned power limit plus about 150 W for the platform, and keep continuous load near 80% of the PSU rating. A 15 A/120 V circuit supports only about 12 A, or 1,440 W, so bigger rigs need 20 A or 240 V [1q_WZwOjByQ @ 00:03:38]. Red Panda Mining builds in headroom the same way, planning only six to eight of ten servers on a rack fed by three 30 A/240 V circuits [mfQE_CptyLA @ 00:15:12]. Heat is the other half of the equation. Modern Mining exhausts rig heat through a window with a 50 W fan. Dumping it indoors roughly doubles the power cost, though it offsets heating in winter [WJnsgbZsg0U @ 00:10:33]. Nobody treats electrical and thermal planning as optional once multiple cards run around the clock.

sections.heading: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Modern Mining's single-card build is the cleanest consumer template for Salad. The parts list: a used ASUS TUF 4090 at $2,100, a no-name 1000 W PSU with a native 12V 600 W cable for about $100, an $80 MSI B550 board, a $90 Ryzen 5500, a $15 frame, a $10 Govee smart plug, 64 GB of used eBay DDR4 for $320, a $20 Peerless Assassin cooler and a 1 TB NVMe [WJnsgbZsg0U @ 00:02:05]. The unit economics are spelled out step by step. Eighteen cents an hour, which Modern Mining calls the cap, equals $4.32 a day. Salad's 10% cash-out fee and a 40-cent deduction cut that to $3.88. Roughly 0.4 kW of draw over 24 hours costs $0.96, leaving $2.92 a day. That is about $854 a year at 80% uptime and a 3.5-year breakeven, before counting 80-90% card resale [WJnsgbZsg0U @ 00:37:51]. BearMarketMiner lists Salad's entry bar as 32 GB RAM, 500 GB storage and about 50 Mb each way. A 5090 prices around 0.237 there, and a 4060 Ti around 6 cents, averaging 7 to 13 cents [egH5hKD913Y @ 00:12:53]. The tuning trick: locking the 7950X at 1600 MHz dropped system draw from 600 W to 318 W. Power-limiting below 90% on Salad, though, gets the rig degraded [egH5hKD913Y @ 00:21:18].

Red Panda Mining runs the opposite playbook: cheap ex-enterprise servers packed with older high-VRAM cards. The core buy was a pallet of ten Gigabyte G481-HA0 servers at $500 each plus $600 freight. The upgrades were Xeon Gold 6152s at about $350 for 22, plus 32 sticks of 16 GB DDR4-2400 ECC RDIMM at $40-50 apiece [mfQE_CptyLA @ 00:12:51]. Into the Gigabyte chassis go eight passively cooled Tesla V100 16 GB cards at about CA$400-420 each. They rent for 8-20 cents an hour, against 8-15 cents for a 5060 Ti that costs nearly CA$1,000 after tax. The V100 buys similar rent at half the price, with a projected $25-40 a day and a 4-6 month ROI [ET1JYocpu0M @ 00:07:02]. The 170HX server is the payoff: ten cards unlocked to 64 GB each for 640 GB of VRAM, rented at 20 cents per GPU per hour. It earned $30.42 for 9 GPUs over 19 hours and $36.37 over about 24 hours. After SimplePod's 20% fee, 20 cents nets about 16 cents, or $38.40 per full day, on cards bought for $150-170 [SJbOF9Ufm0Q @ 00:08:10]. Alec Glover maps the sales channels above that. Vast, RunPod and ShadeForm take about 25%, while resellers such as HydroHost, ShadeForm and FluidStack take 7.5-15% on one-to-two-year contracts [iuLuDflfEE4 @ 00:17:08].

At warehouse scale, Alec Glover's hardware rules come from weeks lost to unstable risers and adapters. Buy ASRock boards with native SlimSAS (19 ports, eight GPUs at x16, a 14-GPU limit), or MCIO for Gen5. Cheap slot-to-SlimSAS adapters threw AER errors and driver crashes after weeks, and 10GTech Gen5 risers failed within 30 minutes. Only C-Payne risers, at over $100 per GPU, and One Chassis assemblies, at about $80, stayed stable [CgsDEFaGLJ0 @ 00:13:22]. Gen4 moves 2 GB/s per lane against Gen5's 4 GB/s, about 24 versus 48 GB/s at x16 in practice. Even so, dropping Gen5 cards into Gen4/DDR4 systems saved roughly $10K per server, and the 5090 inference customer didn't care [CgsDEFaGLJ0 @ 00:05:12]. Red Panda Mining draws the line lower down: no 4090s on Gen3, which the channel calls a waste. Its 8x4090 plan is therefore a 7U PCIe 5.0 MCIO build rather than a reuse of the Gen3 Octominer box [X2uIX3DDPu0 @ 00:07:29]. Crypto LLC adds the riser diagnosis from mining farms. When new cards crash Windows 11 and System interrupts sit at 7-10%, the culprit is 'most of the time' a riser, even though BIOS shows every PCIe port green. Swapping the bad riser dropped interrupts to 0-1% [nHwXk9HCuYI @ 00:04:18].

callout.title: Small moves the rental operators use to squeeze more out of each rig
callout.body: Four field-tested adjustments covering card selection, power draw, used-card buying and vendor quotes.
items: SimplePod wants 30-series cards, not more 4090s or 5090s; 3090s and 3060s rent consistently at low power draw [Red Panda Mining — mfQE_CptyLA @ 00:08:39].
Pin the CPU clock: locking a 7950X at 1600 MHz cut system draw from 600 W to 318 W, but never power-limit below 90% on Salad or the rig gets degraded [BearMarketMiner — egH5hKD913Y @ 00:21:18].
Test used GPUs in person before paying, price-check on gpudeals.net, seat the 12V cable fully and run a 14-gauge power cable [Modern Mining — WJnsgbZsg0U @ 00:14:04].
Play OEMs against each other: Glover cites Dell at $1M versus Supermicro at $750K, with OEM margins around 10% and sometimes 8% [Alec Glover — CgsDEFaGLJ0 @ 00:54:07].

sop_steps.title: Spec the box for what renters filter on
sop_steps.action: Lock in upload bandwidth, system RAM and NVMe storage before choosing the card count.
sop_steps.detail: Run at least 500 Mb, ideally 1 Gb symmetric, because upload matters [Modern Mining — WJnsgbZsg0U @ 00:10:01]. Carry high system RAM: a 63 GB rig got 82 rentals versus 7 at 26 GB [BearMarketMiner — egH5hKD913Y @ 00:10:53].

sop_steps.title: Configure BIOS and remote access for unattended uptime
sop_steps.action: Set BIOS for automatic recovery and install remote and update-blocking tools.
sop_steps.detail: Turn XMP off, set restore after AC power loss to on, and enable SVM. Then install Stop Updates 10, Chrome Remote Desktop and Nvidia drivers [Modern Mining — WJnsgbZsg0U @ 00:23:42].

sop_steps.title: Burn in and hunt down riser faults before listing
sop_steps.action: Stress-test every GPU for days and watch for throttling or interrupt spikes.
sop_steps.detail: Run the C-Payne stress tool for 48 hours to a week and flag drops like a 4090 falling from 450 W to 230 W [Alec Glover — CgsDEFaGLJ0 @ 00:46:26]. On Windows, System interrupts at 7-10% point to a bad riser [Crypto LLC — nHwXk9HCuYI @ 00:01:27].

sop_steps.title: List low, get rented, and clear verification
sop_steps.action: Undercut comparable listings to win first rentals, then relist if the machine stalls unverified.
sop_steps.detail: Red Panda priced a 3080 rig lowest among eight-GPU rigs on Vast and it rented instantly [Red Panda Mining — ET1JYocpu0M @ 00:12:03]. For unverified listings, unlist for 5-10 minutes and relist [Red Panda Mining — mfQE_CptyLA @ 00:07:30].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Alec Glover and Red Panda Mining run opposite hardware playbooks. Glover's rule for any rental business is to buy the newest generation: it costs a premium, depreciates in a friendlier way, and stays rentable longer, while low-end stock is what sits idle when the market slows [CgsDEFaGLJ0 @ 00:01:08]. Looking back on a warehouse cloud scaled to 1,000 GPUs, Glover says the move now would be decommissioned H100s and H200s in a DIY facility that can be certified [iuLuDflfEE4 @ 00:11:02]. Red Panda Mining goes the other way on purpose. They bought a pallet of ten Gigabyte G481-HA0 servers at $500 each, run PCIe 3.0 boards, and openly flag that this gear may command lower rates than AMD Epyc systems [mfQE_CptyLA @ 00:12:51]. Their V100 buy follows the same logic: Tesla V100 16 GB cards at roughly CA$400 to 420 each rent for 8 to 20 cents an hour, against 8 to 15 cents for a 5060 Ti that costs about CA$800 before tax, so the older card earns similar rent for half the capital [ET1JYocpu0M @ 00:07:02]. Glover is optimizing for durability and certification; Red Panda is optimizing for payback speed, targeting a four-to-six-month ROI on the V100 box.

The build-versus-buy line splits by card class. Alec Glover says that for enterprise cards a vendor charges only a 10 to 15 percent margin over building, so paying roughly $10K extra on a $100K server for the warranty is the smart trade, and building only makes sense for consumer GPUs [iuLuDflfEE4 @ 00:03:03]. On bus bandwidth, Glover measured about 24 GB/s on Gen4 x16 versus 48 on Gen5, yet putting Gen5 cards on Gen4/DDR4 hosts saved about $10K per server and their 5090 inference customer never noticed [CgsDEFaGLJ0 @ 00:07:16]. Glover still concedes Gen5 is always more expensive than Gen4 but carries twice the throughput. Red Panda Mining draws a harder line for the top cards: 4090s on a Gen3 Octominer are a waste, so they are planning a separate 7U PCIe 5.0 MCIO build for eight 4090s and reserving the Gen3 box for 3070s or CMP 170HX cards [X2uIX3DDPu0 @ 00:07:29]. Yet the same channel's ten 170HX cards, unlocked to 64 GB each and running LLM inference over a PCIe 2.0 x4 link, are pulling real rentals, matching their own read that renters want multi-GPU nodes to pool VRAM for large LLMs [SJbOF9Ufm0Q @ 00:05:28].

Platform choice is where the playbooks fork hardest. Alec Glover calls the roughly 25 percent cut taken by Vast, RunPod, and ShadeForm cheap, because the marketplace absorbs marketing, sales, and support, while resellers such as HydroHost, ShadeForm, and FluidStack take only 7.5 to 15 percent but want one- to two-year contracts [iuLuDflfEE4 @ 00:15:18]. Red Panda Mining pays that same 25 percent on Vast but splits their fleet: invite-only SimplePod demands redundant internet and generators, wants 30-series cards rather than more 4090s and 5090s, and keeps their 3090s and 3060s rented at low draw, while Vast renters appear to be crypto-mining instead [mfQE_CptyLA @ 00:08:39]. Modern Mining runs Salad instead, accepting a 10 percent cash-out fee plus a 40-cent deduction and an 18-cent hourly cap on a 4090 [WJnsgbZsg0U @ 00:37:51]. BearMarketMiner, after $10,000 of testing, gives the most split verdict: on OctaSpace a 4060 Ti rented about as often as a 5090, so start with a 4060 Ti, yet they also conclude high-end is definitely the way to go, and their Salad 5090 kept earning until its three-month job ended [egH5hKD913Y @ 00:04:39]. The right card depends on which marketplace's renters you are courting.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Risers and boards are where the firsthand losses cluster. Alec Glover's cheap slot-to-SlimSAS adapters threw AER errors and crashed drivers only after weeks in service, and the 10GTech Gen5 risers they tested were completely unusable, failing within 30 minutes, while C-Payne risers at over $100 per GPU and One Chassis assemblies at about $80 stayed stable [CgsDEFaGLJ0 @ 00:13:41]. Their blunt verdict was that they wasted time avoiding ASRock boards with native SlimSAS [iuLuDflfEE4 @ 00:02:25]. Crypto LLC sees the same pattern on Windows 11 farms: three freshly installed GPUs crashed the whole rig as soon as they mined, System interrupts sat at 7 to 13 percent, and BIOS still showed every PCIe port green, falsely signalling all was well. Their fix is to reseat the risers, rerun the miner, then swap one riser at a time, and from their experience it is risers most of the time [nHwXk9HCuYI @ 00:04:18]. Red Panda Mining's 600 CAD Octominer never booted at all: no VGA signal, a flashing LED, and an M1 error after a CMOS reset, RAM and CPU reseats, a swap to E5-2640 V3s, and pulling the NVMe, leaving a motherboard swap on the to-do list [X2uIX3DDPu0 @ 00:16:34].

The second trap is gross-rate math. Alec Glover warns that newcomers simply divide hardware cost by online hourly rates, when a cloud is far more than hardware [iuLuDflfEE4 @ 00:00:18]. Red Panda Mining's own 170HX server shows the gap: the $60-a-day figure was shoot-for-the-moon pricing, while real rentals paid $30.42 for nine GPUs over 19 hours and about $36.37 over a full day, and SimplePod's 20 percent fee turns a 20-cent rate into roughly 16 cents [SJbOF9Ufm0Q @ 00:08:10]. Modern Mining walks the same erosion on Salad: a 4090 capped at 18 cents an hour grosses $4.32 a day, drops to $3.88 after the 10 percent fee and 40-cent deduction, then to $2.92 after power, and at 80 percent uptime lands near $854 a year and a 3.5-year breakeven, which they offset by counting on 80 to 90 percent resale value [WJnsgbZsg0U @ 00:39:50]. Mining-side operators face a faster squeeze: MysticOrb289's 3090 is barely covering power on Quantus at 22 cents per kWh, and a working FPGA bitstream for the Osprey E-300 now threatens the GPU miners, with daily coin output halving if difficulty doubles [w5vhWKlqN_k @ 00:01:21].

Network and power shortcuts break under real load. Alec Glover's earlier network ran daisy-chained 1G links to single ports on each machine and caused outages, so they rebuilt around redundant routers, MC-LAG switch pairs, and Arista 10G 48-port switches at about $200 each [iuLuDflfEE4 @ 00:10:03]. Red Panda Mining hit the same wall at smaller scale when a renter pulled 400 GB in 20 minutes over 3 Gb fiber: throughput swung between 550 Mbps and 3 Gbps, packet loss hit 10 to 12 percent, and an X550 NIC firmware error surfaced, leaving a possible Ubiquiti upgrade on the table [SJbOF9Ufm0Q @ 00:12:23]. On power, Glover keeps every circuit, PSU, and PDU at a consistent 80 percent load and burns in new servers for 48 hours to a week, because a 4090 sliding from 450 W to 230 W can crash on overheating or throttle an entire multi-GPU server back [CgsDEFaGLJ0 @ 00:47:22]. BearMarketMiner flags two settings that quietly kill income: power-limiting below 90 percent on Salad gets the rig degraded, and thin RAM starves demand, with a 26 GB rig landing 7 rentals in about 30 days against 82 for a 63 GB rig [egH5hKD913Y @ 00:10:53].

chapters.question_prompt: What hardware actually sits inside AI compute capacity, and how do H100, H200, B200, and alternative accelerators differ for buyers and renters?
chapters.title: Inside the Silicon: Data-Center GPUs, AI Servers, and Challenger Chips
chapters.subtitle: Modding a CMP 170HX into an A100, modern AI server anatomy, an 8-GPU DGX V100 in colo, H100 internals, H100 vs H200 vs B200 inference specs, a Lambda B200 cluster tour, Dell XE9680 and Supermicro HGX 8-GPU systems, IBM's 288-card design, a wafer-scale '30x faster' chip, Stanford's memory claim, and Intel's AI-stack gap
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners converge on one verdict: in data-center AI silicon, memory capacity and bandwidth price the asset, not headline teraflops. Hitesh C., Screwdriver Science and AI Andrew all show H100-class parts starving at under one percent utilization during decode, while Cloud Ninjas and Supermicro confirm the tradeable unit is an 8-GPU SXM/HGX baseboard with a 1:1 GPU-to-NIC ratio. Street mechanics run from SysTelligence's ipmitool fan override and a 1,000-hour payback on a $250K box, to LOCKBREAK's $8 voltage-glitch board turning a $2,500 CMP 170HX into 80 GB and 85.9 TF. Disagreements are sharp: Cyfuture AI claims the H200 runs up to 45% faster, Gimel12 measured near-parity on Ollama, and AI Andrew plus Tomorrow Engineered argue challenger chips beat GPUs on energy per token.

sections.heading: Section 1 - The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator on this bench lands in the same place: the scarce resource inside an AI server is memory capacity and bandwidth, not raw flops. Hitesh C. pins the H100 at 80 GB of HBM3 moving 3.35 TB/s with FP8 at 3,958 TF and FP16 at 1,979 TF, then warns that both headline numbers are sparse figures that halve the moment you run dense [fKrvPg4P6KY @ 00:00:28]. Screwdriver Science explains why that matters physically: a memory fetch burns roughly 100 times the energy of a multiply, so the H100 stacks HBM twelve-high at more than 1 TB/s per stack and uses eight stacks to reach about 8 TB/s, all inside a module that pulls about 700 W [b3RlbR2xqfM @ 00:07:32]. AI Andrew runs the roofline that closes the argument: Llama 3 8B in FP16 is 16 GB of weights, one full read at 3.35 TB/s takes 4.8 ms, and because the H100 wants about 295 operations per byte while token-by-token decode delivers about one, utilization sits under one percent [vj8GAlW7mQo @ 00:02:42]. Extrude Studio reaches the same conclusion from the other side, reporting compute idle up to 80% of the time under autoregression on $30,000-plus cards [xkHs2GUaKro @ 00:01:18].

The second agreement is about physical shape, and it dictates what you can actually buy and resell. Scott Flowers is blunt that SXM5 and HGX parts are not discrete cards: "you're going to see a baseboard as opposed to a PCIe card," one board carrying all eight GPUs, with the host's ten PCIe slots allocated as one NIC per GPU plus two for networking [NvI2zdq5I3Q @ 00:02:09]. Supermicro states the same topology as a design rule, putting 400 GB NICs into eight PCIe x16 slots to give "a 1:1 GPU to Nick ratio to avoid Network bottlenecks," then aggregating 32 nodes onto a non-blocking spine-leaf fabric [K7eFRXwd_9U @ 00:00:57]. Murli quantifies why the baseboard exists at all: NVLink moves 900 GB/s while PCIe 5.0 manages 64 GB/s, and ConnectX-7 is what enables GPUDirect RDMA out of the box [2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:02:47]. ServeTheHome shows the generational step in the same slot: B200 HGX runs eight ConnectX-7 at 400 Gb, one per GPU, while B300 moves to ConnectX-8 at 800 Gb per GPU built directly into the baseboard, doubling network throughput and bringing 288 GB of HBM3E per part [CHEbom4opXg @ 00:03:13].

Third, the baseline prerequisite is not the GPU budget, it is power and heat, and most rooms do not have either. Screwdriver Science puts 72 GPUs in a rack at about 120 kW, roughly a hundred homes, and calls a single H100 module "a microwave oven running flat out all day" [b3RlbR2xqfM @ 00:10:20]. Murli does the same math at the chassis level: eight 700 W parts is 5,600 W before overhead, the server exceeds 10,000 W in practice, air-cooled models need inlet air below 30 degrees, and "hot aisle containment is mandatory" because the hot aisle exceeds 70 degrees [2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:07:25]. ServeTheHome walks the plant that answers this, an in-row CDU rated at about 1.8 MW, "enough for more than 10 of these NBL 72 racks," plus rear-door heat exchangers at 50 kW and 80 kW and cooling towers that push water toward ambient rather than refrigerating it [CHEbom4opXg @ 00:12:14], and calls liquid cooling "standard in 18 months" at Lambda's 36 MW Columbus site [N5AJJ0tAoxc @ 00:01:23]. AI Andrew supplies the gap that makes this a sourcing problem: 69% of operators still run racks under 10 kW [vj8GAlW7mQo @ 00:07:38].

sections.heading: Section 2 - Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Start with the spec-and-price ladder the sellers themselves quote. Hitesh C. puts the H200 at 141 GB and 4.8 TB/s with identical compute to the H100 and NVLink at 900, giving a decode ceiling about 1.4x higher, and flags that the widely repeated Llama 2 70B 1.9x result compares batch 32 against batch 8 [fKrvPg4P6KY @ 00:01:18]. Cyfuture AI frames the same part as +76% VRAM and +43% memory speed inside the same 700 W envelope, claims up to 45% faster LLM inference and 1.7x in multi-GPU, then prices it at 20-25% more than an H100 with cloud rental starting around $3.80 per hour and the pitch that "total cost per workload can actually be lower" [8nL31VyVz8s @ 00:01:00]. Design Guy scores B200 over H200 six rounds to two: 180 GB against 141 GB, 7.7 TB/s against 4.8, FP8 at 9 PF sparse against 3,958 TF, but 1,000 W against 700 W and FP64 falling to 37 TF from 67 TF [PnUJffgghas @ 00:05:35]. Gimel12 supplies the street price floor, calling H100 and H200 "30 or 30 something" thousand and hard to find, against an A6000 at roughly $7-8K delivering 17.5 tok/s [gD-lTOjHc04 @ 00:06:54].

The most aggressive mechanic in this chapter is LOCKBREAK's account of Kate turning mining silicon into A100-class compute. The CMP 170HX carries the same GA100 die as a $20,000-plus A100; GA100 has 128 SMs and retail A100 enables 108, while the mining SKU launched in 2021 at $4,299 crippled to 70 SMs, 8 GB usable memory, PCIe Gen1, no NVLink and a 1/32 math rate enforced by 16,384 eFuses, even though about 80 GB of HBM2E is physically present [k-M24u2WcZw @ 00:01:25]. Munikote's CMP Unlocker, following Pry's "A Canary in the Crypto Mine" paper, exposed 64 GB, restored math and doubled link speed, pushing card prices from a couple hundred dollars to over $1,000, but it could not touch fuses [k-M24u2WcZw @ 00:03:26]. The hardware path is voltage glitching with an roughly $8 microcontroller board that controls the VRM and dips power during the fuse read to disable write-protect, after which new fuse records clear the disable masks while leaving genuinely defective cores off, taking one hour to two days per card [k-M24u2WcZw @ 00:04:23]. Nine of ten cards hit 80 GB with 120-126 SMs [k-M24u2WcZw @ 00:05:44].

On the operations side the tooling is specific and short. Murli overrides thermals with `ipmitool raw 0x30 0x45 0x01 0x01` to pin fans at full speed for training runs [2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:08:08], caps draw with `nvidia-smi -p`, plans electrical for 120% of nameplate load [2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:09:34], keeps IPMI on a separate out-of-band VLAN because "mixing IPMI management traffic with GPU workload traffic causes serious performance issues," holds GPUs below 83 degrees and HBM below 95, treats memory use above 90% as near capacity, and keeps 200 Gb InfiniBand off the management switch [2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:05:17]. Craft Computing's version of the same discipline is version-pinning: Proxmox 8 with GRID 17.6, because 19 drops V100 and 18 is unstable, and 17.6 demands kernel 6.8 or lower, which rules out Proxmox 9, on an Inspur DGX V100 that idles near 950 W and hits 3,300 W loaded with GRID entry licensing at $3,000 or $10,000 [9c1c3JPZ2ps @ 00:05:19]. Scott Flowers closes the resale loop: an order for 1,000 units is "very difficult," they filled 128 with painful OEM matching, and held value beats their ROI models [NvI2zdq5I3Q @ 00:05:08].

callout.title: Four moves the practitioners actually executed and measured
callout.body: These are the specific, repeatable levers the speakers demonstrated on live hardware, with the numbers they recorded and the limits they hit while doing it.
items: Treat sparse spec sheets as marketing: sparse figures are exactly double the dense figures, and the entire B200 number set is still 'projected' by the vendor, so pick H200 when KV cache limits batch size and Blackwell only when you genuinely need FP4 or faster NVLink [Hitesh C. — fKrvPg4P6KY @ 00:03:01].

Keep the baseboard in the chassis. Scott Flowers refuses the job outright - 'I do not like to take the baseboard out. I just don't.' - because only a few removals are safe, and he will not even film an install until a failed unit shows up [Cloud Ninjas — NvI2zdq5I3Q @ 00:00:32].

Isolate management traffic and harden the box before it leaves your hands: IPMI on its own out-of-band VLAN, 200 Gb InfiniBand off the management switch, secure boot enabled and NVMe encrypted, with electrical planned at 120 percent of load [SysTelligence — 2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:05:17].

Do not trust a single-framework benchmark to price silicon. Running Llama 3.3 70B at Q4 under Ollama produced 36.6 tok/s on an H100 and effectively no gain on an H200 at 87-90 percent utilization, which the operator attributes to the inference server and plans to retest on vLLM [Gimel12 — gD-lTOjHc04 @ 00:03:51].

sop_steps.title: Fix the memory budget before shopping for compute
sop_steps.action: Compute weights plus KV cache for the target model, then select the part by capacity and bandwidth rather than flops.
sop_steps.detail: A 70B model needs roughly 140 GB, which is why H100 at 80 GB forces sharding while H200 at 141 GB and 4.8 TB/s or B200 at 192 GB do not [SysTelligence — 2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:04:12]; FP16 at that size wants about 132 GB, so Q4 quantization drops the same model to roughly 43 GB and changes the whole hardware decision [Gimel12 — gD-lTOjHc04 @ 00:01:29].

sop_steps.title: Buy the system as a baseboard plus fabric, never as loose parts
sop_steps.action: Specify an 8-GPU SXM/HGX baseboard with one NIC per GPU and confirm slot count before the purchase order.
sop_steps.detail: Expect ten PCIe slots allocated as one NIC per GPU plus two for networking on a single eight-GPU baseboard [Cloud Ninjas — NvI2zdq5I3Q @ 00:03:25], matched to eight 400 GB NICs in eight x16 slots for a 1:1 GPU-to-NIC ratio and 32-node non-blocking spine-leaf aggregation [Supermicro — K7eFRXwd_9U @ 00:00:57].

sop_steps.title: Prove the power and cooling envelope on paper first
sop_steps.action: Add up PSU capacity, inlet temperature limits and containment, then size the plant for the real rack draw.
sop_steps.detail: Plan on 4,000 to 6,000 W power supplies, inlet air below 30 degrees for air-cooled units, and a chassis that exceeds 10,000 W once eight 700 W parts and fans are running [SysTelligence — 2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:02:05]; at rack scale that becomes six 5,250 W titanium supplies per server and 130 kg of weight inside 1.6 MW UPS blocks [ServeTheHome — N5AJJ0tAoxc @ 00:08:31].

sop_steps.title: Run the buy-versus-rent arithmetic both ways before committing
sop_steps.action: Price the box against hourly rental at realistic utilization, then sanity-check against resale behaviour.
sop_steps.detail: A roughly $250K server against $240 per hour of equivalent rental pays back in about 1,000 hours, while the same operator states typical enterprise break-even runs 12 to 18 months [SysTelligence — 2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:13:01]; three-year-old H100s and H200s are 'still monsters' whose held value beats the ROI models, with H200s scarce because hyperscalers are holding them [Cloud Ninjas — NvI2zdq5I3Q @ 00:06:10].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split in Hopper buying is how much the H200 actually buys you. Cyfuture AI pitches the card as up to 45% faster on LLM inference and 1.7x in multi-GPU runs inside the same 700 W envelope. It argues that a 20–25% price premium and cloud entry near $3.80/hr still produce a lower cost per workload [Cyfuture AI — 8nL31VyVz8s @ 00:00:40]. Gimel12 ran Llama 3.3 70B at Q4 on Ollama with Open WebUI and got 36.6 tok/s on the H100, with the H200 landing in the same band. Both cards pulled about 600 W at 87–90% utilization. The speaker's verdict was 'not a big difference,' which they blamed on the Ollama inference server; they called the result inaccurate and promised a vLLM rerun [Gimel12 — gD-lTOjHc04 @ 00:03:51]. Hitesh C. sits between the two. Compute is the same, but memory goes from 80 GB at 3.35 TB/s to 141 GB at 4.8 TB/s, so the decode ceiling rises about 1.4x. Nvidia's 1.9x Llama 2 70B headline compares batch 32 against batch 8 [Hitesh C. — fKrvPg4P6KY @ 00:01:18]. The working read: the H200 premium pays off when the extra memory lets you raise batch size, not when a quantized model already fits in 80 GB.

On the Hopper-versus-Blackwell call, Design Guy scores the B200 a 6–2 winner. It has 180 GB versus 141 GB, 7.7 TB/s versus 4.8 TB/s, 9 PF sparse FP8 versus 3,958 TF, and 1.8 TB/s NVLink versus 900 GB/s. The H200 keeps two rounds: FP64, at 67 TF against 37 TF, and power, at 700 W against 1,000 W TDP. That keeps FP64 shops and tight power envelopes on the H200 [Design Guy — PnUJffgghas @ 00:05:35]. Hitesh C. frames the same fork as a workload rule. If KV cache is what caps batch size, buy H200; if you need FP4 or faster NVLink, buy Blackwell. B200 figures are Nvidia projections, and sparse numbers are double the dense ones [Hitesh C. — fKrvPg4P6KY @ 00:03:01]. Cloud Ninjas argues the older iron is far from dead: resale values on three-year-old H100 and H200 servers have held up and beaten ROI models [Cloud Ninjas — NvI2zdq5I3Q @ 00:06:10]. Gimel12 takes the budget road entirely. The A6000 clocked 17.5 tok/s at roughly $7–8K, against H100 or H200 cards at '30 or 30 something' thousand that are hard to find. For multi-user load, Gimel12 often recommends two to four A6000s [Gimel12 — gD-lTOjHc04 @ 00:08:29].

The challenger camp splits on whether Nvidia's lead is the silicon or the stack. Tomorrow Engineered relays Cerebras claims of up to 30x over Nvidia GPUs and an Artificial Analysis run of more than 2,500 tok/s on Llama 4 Maverick, against roughly 1,000 for Blackwell and 550 for Groq. SemiAnalysis pegs the real gap at 20–40x and calls the efficiency gain 'slight at best' on 125–135 kW racks [Tomorrow Engineered — yYBoW-BKDl8 @ 00:16:36]. AI Andrew pushes IBM's NorthPole, a 288-card 12 nm rack drawing about 30 kW air-cooled that claims 72.7x less energy per token than the H100. He then concedes it is a capacity-limited, inference-only prototype that IBM itself benchmarked against Hopper and 2024-era vLLM [AI Andrew — vj8GAlW7mQo @ 00:28:28]. Extrude Studio argues the fix belongs in the model rather than the chip. Next concept modeling from Hazy Research turns a 1,000-word answer into 32 parallel passes for roughly 30x, versus 2–3x from speculative decoding [Extrude Studio — xkHs2GUaKro @ 00:04:32]. CyberPulse answers every hardware story with the moat thesis. Intel lost with Larrabee, Xeon Phi, Gaudi 3 and Falcon Shores because Nvidia sells 'the promise' of compatibility. CyberPulse adds that PyTorch and AI-written code are now lowering switching costs [CyberPulse — Z69EERVnY6w @ 00:14:29].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The hardware-unlock trade is the sharpest example of one-way risk. LOCKBREAK walks through Kate's voltage-glitch workflow on CMP 170HX mining cards. An ~$8 microcontroller board dips VRM power during the fuse read to disable write-protect. New fuse records then clear the disable masks while truly defective cores stay off, at one hour to two days per card [LOCKBREAK — k-M24u2WcZw @ 00:04:23]. The traps are spelled out on camera. Fuse writes are permanent, and 'No driver update can unblow a fuse.' Results are a lottery: 9 of 10 cards reached 80 GB with 120–126 SMs, but one topped out at 64 GB. The 85.9 TF headline comes from a single non-tensor OpenCL FP16 test, sits only about 10% above the 78 TF spec, and ECC and MIG were never tested [LOCKBREAK — k-M24u2WcZw @ 00:07:03]. The margin also compresses fast. The software unlock alone pushed cards from a couple hundred dollars to over $1,000, and the 10 GB card now sits near $2,500 with the 8 GB near $3,000 [LOCKBREAK — k-M24u2WcZw @ 00:09:11]. Cloud Ninjas applies the same irreversibility logic to HGX servers. They refuse to pull baseboards because only a few removals are safe, and they are holding off on an install walkthrough until they have a failed unit [Cloud Ninjas — NvI2zdq5I3Q @ 00:00:32].

Hosting traps hit before any revenue lands. Craft Computing's eight-V100 DGX cloud-gaming build is pinned to Proxmox 8 and GRID 17.6. Version 19 dropped V100, version 18 is unstable, and 17.6 needs kernel 6.8 or older, which locks out Proxmox 9. The vGPU unlock only spans Maxwell through Turing/Volta [Craft Computing — 9c1c3JPZ2ps @ 00:05:19]. Once running, GRID caps output at 60 FPS and VRAM splits statically. VMs cost about 10%, plus 5% for GRID. The box idles near 950 W and hits 3,300 W at full load. The verdict was disappointing: roughly a GTX 1070 per gamer. GRID entry costs $3,000 for an A5000 or $10,000 for a Blackwell 6000 Pro, while Intel's B70 Pro offers SR-IOV with no licensing [Craft Computing — 9c1c3JPZ2ps @ 00:17:04]. SysTelligence lists the data-center failure points. Mixing IPMI management traffic with GPU workload traffic 'causes serious performance issues.' GPUs must stay under 83°C and HBM under 95°C. Hot aisles exceed 70°C, so containment is mandatory, and power should be planned at 120% of load [SysTelligence — 2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:05:17]. ServeTheHome adds that a 1.8 MW in-row CDU needs its pH, inlet and outlet temperatures, and pump speeds watched [ServeTheHome — CHEbom4opXg @ 00:12:14].

Supply and concentration risk is the economics check most buyers skip. Cloud Ninjas trades used H100 through B300 servers. They report that H200s are scarce because hyperscalers are holding them, while H100s only trickle out. An order for 1,000 is 'very difficult,' and even a filled order of 128 was hard because OEM and configuration had to match [Cloud Ninjas — NvI2zdq5I3Q @ 00:05:08]. AI Andrew flags HBM as the choke point: it is sold out through 2026, and the squeeze is expected to run to late 2027. He also notes that 69% of operators run racks under 10 kW, while an NVL72 costs about $3M and draws about 120 kW [AI Andrew — vj8GAlW7mQo @ 00:07:38]. Tomorrow Engineered stacks up the Cerebras warnings. Memory has been stuck at 44 GB since 2021. DeepSeek V4 Pro needs about 40 systems, over $20M and 1 MW. The prefill/decode hardware ratio is fixed at order time. UAE customers made up 86% of 2025 revenue [Tomorrow Engineered — yYBoW-BKDl8 @ 00:19:11]. CyberPulse shows what a stack miss costs. Gaudi 3 missed $500M, Intel posted a $16.6B quarterly loss and an $18.8B annual loss, Intel was dropped from the Dow, and Falcon Shores was cancelled [CyberPulse — Z69EERVnY6w @ 00:08:39].

callout.title: Stop Checks Before Committing Capital to GPU Iron
callout.body: Each of these failures was hit or measured firsthand by an operator. Clear all four before you buy, flash, or rack anything.
items: Do not write fuse records on any card you cannot afford to brick: fuse writes are permanent and unlock yields vary, with one card stuck at 64 GB [LOCKBREAK — k-M24u2WcZw @ 00:08:13].
Confirm the GRID branch and kernel before building vGPU hosts: 17.6 needs kernel 6.8 or older, and version 19 drops V100 [Craft Computing — 9c1c3JPZ2ps @ 00:05:19].
Put IPMI on a separate out-of-band VLAN, keep InfiniBand off the management switch, and hold GPUs under 83°C before loading training jobs [SysTelligence — 2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:05:17].
Do not promise large H200 deliveries until OEM and configuration matches are secured; 1,000-unit orders are very difficult and even 128 was hard [Cloud Ninjas — NvI2zdq5I3Q @ 00:05:08].

chapters.pull_quote: "No driver update can unblow a fuse." — LOCKBREAK (k-M24u2WcZw @ 00:07:03)
action_checklist: Rerun any H100-versus-H200 comparison on vLLM instead of Ollama before trusting a near-parity result [Gimel12 — gD-lTOjHc04 @ 00:03:51].
Halve sparse TFLOPS figures to get dense throughput, and treat B200 numbers as Nvidia projections when sizing a purchase [Hitesh C. — fKrvPg4P6KY @ 00:03:01].
Isolate IPMI on a separate out-of-band VLAN so management traffic never mixes with GPU workload traffic [SysTelligence — 2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:05:17].
Cap GPU power with nvidia-smi -p and size power delivery at 120% of the expected load [SysTelligence — 2tGJAc9AgQI @ 00:09:14].
Spec one 400 Gb NIC per GPU across the 8 PCIe x16 slots to hold a 1:1 GPU-to-NIC ratio and avoid network bottlenecks [Supermicro — K7eFRXwd_9U @ 00:00:57].
Pin V100 vGPU hosts to Proxmox 8 with GRID 17.6 on kernel 6.8 or older, since version 19 dropped V100 and version 18 is unstable [Craft Computing — 9c1c3JPZ2ps @ 00:05:19].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I rent the cheapest reliable GPU on RunPod, Vast.ai, and other clouds without getting burned by hidden costs and failed pods?
chapters.title: Renting GPUs on Marketplaces: RunPod vs Vast.ai in the Field
chapters.subtitle: Cheapest GPU per job, $2.69 vs $12.29 H100 price spreads, measured H200 rentals, RTX 4090 pre-rental checks, multi-GPU VRAM traps, 47 of 291 Vast pods that never ran, storage billing on stopped pods, total-job cost traps, and Isaac Sim WebRTC setup
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners split marketplace GPU rental along one line: Vast.ai wins the sticker, RunPod wins the invoice you can predict. GPU Battle found Vast cheaper on 17 of 24 shared cards with 55 of 62 tracked GPUs listed, yet 47 of 291 Vast pods never ran and one 4090 host delivered half speed. Bryan Software tallied 30 to 60% hidden uplift plus $5 to $50 in bandwidth on Vast against RunPod's zero egress, fixed $0.34 4090 rate, and $80-per-hour default spend cap. HostingCompared with Natalie prices jobs on four numbers: total price, reliability, duration, and data costs, warning that stopped storage keeps billing. The street mechanics are consistent: price the job not the hour, vet every host in the first minute, destroy rather than stop. The split is ratio, not winner: GPU Battle runs roughly 70% RunPod, 30% Vast.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus: Vast Wins the Sticker, RunPod Wins the Predictable Bill
paragraphs: Every operator who has spent real money on both platforms describes the same structural split. Bryan Software frames it before running five head-to-head tests: RunPod is a managed GPU cloud with fixed rates and compliance coverage, while Vast.ai is a marketplace where independent hosts set the price [Ez2jsa33jFY @ 00:00:15]. GPU Battle, who checks both price lists every day for a tracker covering 62 cards, found Vast listing 55 of them against RunPod's 31, and where both carried the same card, Vast came in cheaper 17 out of 24 times, with the RTX 3090 at 14 cents versus 22 cents, the RTX 5090 at 45 cents versus 69 cents, and the RTX 5080 at 22 cents versus 39 cents [156XFkwFpwY @ 00:01:16]. The same operator calls Vast the cheapest and also the most expensive provider, because it is the only one where bandwidth pricing shifts with each host, which makes it the pick for cheap low-VRAM consumer cards while RunPod stays the best all-rounder for medium to high workloads [SqfQZYYMPj4 @ 00:01:30]. TWiz reaches the same verdict from the usability side: RunPod for a user-friendly interface and straightforward pricing, Vast for extensive customization and potentially lower costs, paid for with a steeper learning curve on the marketplace model [_UBOzLyl2b0 @ 00:02:05].

The second point of agreement is that the Vast discount is a host lottery, and RunPod does not lose every price fight. GPU Battle's plot twist was RunPod winning on several big cards, with the H100 at $2.69 against $3.59 on Vast, the RTX 4090 at 34 cents against 40 cents, and the A6000 at 33 cents against 40 cents, then watching one Vast 4090 host run at half speed because it was underclocked [156XFkwFpwY @ 00:01:37]. Across 291 Vast rentals the channel logged 47 pods that never ran a single test, a 16% dud rate against 14 out of 200, about 7%, on RunPod, while noting the duds together cost only a dollar [kvP__Lh53oM @ 00:00:17]. The West Reviews relays the same pattern from developers: one Reddit user found Vast's cheap GPUs attractive but saw machines fail mid-job and require restarts, while another found RunPod more stable with more predictable performance and fewer unexpected shutdowns [ZNRLXhDdbW4 @ 00:00:39]. HostingCompared with Natalie turns this into an order of operations: set a reliability minimum before sorting by price, because if one retry ruins the deadline the lowest row becomes the most expensive decision, and even a 99.78% host score is useful history, not magic [cEAhnKuawL8 @ 00:00:40].

The third consensus is about what the bill actually measures, and every speaker says the hourly rate alone lies. Bryan Software notes both platforms bill per second, so a 16-minute job at $1.99 per hour costs 53 cents rather than the full $1.99, a mechanic identical on both sides [Ez2jsa33jFY @ 00:01:25]. GPU Battle flags pricing the hour instead of the job as a core mistake, since per-second billing means a faster card can be cheaper per job, and in their earlier LLM token testing the RTX 3090 rather than the H100 came out cheapest per million tokens [WhTJ6B-YCmw @ 00:04:46]. HostingCompared with Natalie insists on writing down four numbers before launch, productive compute, paid idle time, storage lifetime and expected transfer, and points out that if setup takes five minutes but the GPU sits idle for two hours, setup was never the expensive part [_VqIjD7qiIg @ 00:01:43]. The same channel hammers the exit discipline everyone repeats: stop on RunPod releases the GPU but the volume disk keeps billing at 20 cents per gigabyte per month, so 100 gigabytes is $20 a month, a separate network volume survives even termination, and on Vast stopping halts compute while storage keeps billing as long as the machine is online [OQpEhkeZZp4 @ 00:00:19].

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers: Vetting Scripts, Whole-Job Math, and Storage Discipline
paragraphs: GPU Battle runs rentals through an AI coding agent in Visual Studio Code holding the provider API keys, and the street mechanic is a written instruction set the agent must follow, starting with confirming CPU specs and current RAM before any job lands [WhTJ6B-YCmw @ 00:04:15]. The first trap is power-capped cards that listings never disclose: a 5090 throttled to 450 watts out of 575, a 4090 at 420 watts, a 3090 at 250 watts against 315, plus cheap 3060s sitting behind retired mining rigs on 2016-era CPUs where a host hands over 16 of 64 cores and the job loads forever, then fails to compile [dWC3n2Bn3r8 @ 00:02:25]. The fix is the search prompt itself: search by quality, not price, reliability 99% plus, 16 plus CPU cores, 800 plus megabytes per second, data center host preferred, price the whole job, check power limit, CPU and download speed in the first two minutes, destroy the machine if anything is off, always destroy, never stop, and keep the API key in a local folder instead of pasting it into chat [dWC3n2Bn3r8 @ 00:05:11]. The same channel's one-minute check caught a 4090 drawing 350 watts against a stock 450, and a listing promising about 3 gigabits down that pulled only 14 megabytes a second from Hugging Face [kvP__Lh53oM @ 00:00:53].

The unit economics only work when the whole job is priced line by line. HostingCompared with Natalie models a 36-hour run with four paid idle hours, 100 gigabytes kept seven days and 50 gigabytes downloaded: RunPod compute at the public 74-cent 4090 rate is $29.60 and the full job lands around $33.71 with no transfer fee, while the Vast compute floor at a 28.6-cent host is $11.44, so Vast still wins only if that host's disk and transfer extras stay below roughly $22 [cEAhnKuawL8 @ 00:01:40]. Bryan Software puts the marketplace range at 2 cents to $6.25 per hour depending on host, with hidden costs adding 30 to 60% to the base fee and bandwidth and egress tacking on another $5 to $50, against RunPod's zero egress [Ez2jsa33jFY @ 00:01:06]. GPU Battle shows how fast those line items bite: on one Vast 4090, 6 cents of a 17-cent bill was the download charge, and one bad host running ten times slower wipes out the whole discount [kvP__Lh53oM @ 00:01:44]. That is why the channel says a 53-cent host can beat a 47-cent host, because slow startup on weak CPUs and thin RAM is still billed on the same clock [dWC3n2Bn3r8 @ 00:04:28].

Setup time is the hidden meter, and the speakers attack it with storage choices. GPU Battle warns that downloading a 50 GB model on a GPU pod bills GPU hours the whole time, so the model goes on a network volume and gets downloaded once [WhTJ6B-YCmw @ 00:03:59]. hrithik verma, running Isaac Sim from a public Docker template with an 80 GB disk, measured instance builds of 15 to 20 minutes plus another long wait for the first Isaac Sim load on both platforms, even though data center hosts booted noticeably faster, and recommends volume mounts or storing the instance for a week of work instead of reloading every session [CkxWiz2Qzi8 @ 00:33:04]. On spec selection, HostingCompared with Natalie tells renters of multi-GPU offers to check GPU type and count on RunPod, and on Vast the GPU count, per-GPU memory, total listed memory, PCIe or NVLink bandwidth and total hourly cost, because two 24 GB cards only act like one 48 GB pool when the exact framework supports model or tensor parallelism [b0fXfKwASvI @ 00:01:37]. Data Receipts applies the same discipline at the H100 tier: compare inside one SKU only, since the SXM 80 GB, PCIe 80 GB and NVL 94 GB all get sold as an H100 [ewu0un1Iy8g @ 00:00:49].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split is over which platform deserves to be the default. GPU Battle, who rents across both every day, refuses to crown a winner and lands on a 70/30 mix: 70% of jobs go to RunPod for consistency, templates like PyTorch and ComfyUI, and serverless in one account, while 30% go to Vast for consumer cards RunPod does not stock, benchmarking experiments, and deal sniping on oddities like a Titan RTX [156XFkwFpwY @ 00:06:11]. In a later video the same operator softens that into a pure 'either or' call, picking whichever platform posts the better deal that day and noting the RTX 4090 was actually cheaper on RunPod [WhTJ6B-YCmw @ 00:07:07]. Bryan Software is far less diplomatic: across five decision tests the scoreboard closed RunPod 4, Vast.ai 1, with Vast winning only the raw hourly price test while RunPod took reliability, infrastructure stability, pricing predictability, and container customization [Ez2jsa33jFY @ 00:08:01]. Meanwhile GPU Battle also calls Vast the ultimate value pack for consumer GPUs and budget H100s, provided the agent renting on your API key is told how to dodge the marketplace's traps [dWC3n2Bn3r8 @ 00:02:04]. The operator takeaway is that the headline verdict depends entirely on whether you score sticker price or total predictability.

Practitioners also disagree on whether Vast is actually cheaper once the full bill lands. GPU Battle's own tracking found Vast cheaper 17 out of 24 times where both platforms carry the card, with the RTX 3090 at 14 cents versus 22 cents and the RTX 5090 at 45 cents versus 69 cents, but RunPod won on the big boys, posting the H100 at 2.69 against Vast's 3.59 and the A6000 at 33 cents against 40 cents [156XFkwFpwY @ 00:01:16]. HostingCompared with Natalie frames it differently: RunPod's public RTX 4090 pod rate of 74 cents an hour looks terrible beside a dated Vast host at 28.6 cents, yet that Vast card explicitly says plus bandwidth, so the cheap number is a starting line, not the invoice [cEAhnKuawL8 @ 00:00:19]. Bryan Software puts a number on the gap, claiming Vast's hidden costs add 30 to 60% to the base fee before bandwidth and egress tack on another $5 to $50, while RunPod charges zero for egress [Ez2jsa33jFY @ 00:01:06]. Data Receipts pushes the argument up-market, showing the same H100 SXM ranging from 2.69 to 12.29 an hour, and arguing most of that 4.57x spread is InfiniBand interconnect that a single-node fine-tune will never touch [ewu0un1Iy8g @ 00:02:21].

The sharpest playbook clash is over who Vast is for. GPU Battle slots Vast into small AI workloads on cheap, low-VRAM consumer cards where you will not burn bandwidth, RunPod into medium-to-high workloads, and Modal into the really large B300 projects with 200 GB models [SqfQZYYMPj4 @ 00:03:20]. TWiz flips part of that logic, pitching RunPod's simplicity to small startups while arguing Vast's customization and marketplace model can lead to significant cost savings for larger projects and research teams with specific GPU requirements [_UBOzLyl2b0 @ 00:01:47]. hrithik verma, running Isaac Sim in the cloud, judges the platforms on plumbing rather than price: Vast gives you a full Ubuntu VM and UDP ports for WebRTC streaming through Tailscale, while RunPod offers neither, so streams feel less stable, although both still land about 10x cheaper than the $5 to $6 an hour cited for AWS-style instances [CkxWiz2Qzi8 @ 00:35:07]. The West Reviews relays a split of developer reports: one user liked Vast's cheap GPUs but hit machines failing mid job, while another found RunPod more stable with fewer unexpected shutdowns [ZNRLXhDdbW4 @ 00:00:39]. Pick the platform by workload size, network needs, and how much restarting you can stomach.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure mode is trusting a single marketplace host. GPU Battle rented 291 Vast pods and 47 never ran a single test, a 16% dud rate against 14 out of 200, about 7%, on RunPod; the duds were cheap, costing a dollar combined, so the fix was simply delete and grab another [kvP__Lh53oM @ 00:00:17]. The real damage came from hosts that did run but ran slow: the same operator rented a 4090 that drew 350 watts when a stock 4090 is 450, and listing disk speeds ranged from about 180 megabytes a second to over 30,000 [kvP__Lh53oM @ 00:00:53]. Old machines behind cheap cards are the second trap, with 3060s often sitting on retired mining rigs with 2016-era CPUs where the host hands over 16 of 64 cores, so jobs load forever and then fail to compile [dWC3n2Bn3r8 @ 00:03:06]. Newer cards are not immune: every 5060 GPU Battle tried to rent came back underclocked, saddled with a crappy CPU, or short on RAM, making it useless for testing [WhTJ6B-YCmw @ 00:07:40]. The economics check is blunt: duds cost pennies, slow hosts cost real money, and one bad host can wipe out the whole discount.

Interruptible capacity is where cheap turns into lost work. GPU Battle bid on Vast spot pods 17 times and eight got kicked off before they finished, about half, which the operator rates great for a quick test and terrible for anything you cannot restart [kvP__Lh53oM @ 00:01:13]. Bryan Software describes the nightmare version: a training run spins up, runs 40 minutes, the host drops, and you lose both the compute time and the checkpoint, with Vast's provisioning score at 3.6 out of five and no platform-wide contractual SLA [Ez2jsa33jFY @ 00:02:38]. Worse, the same operator flags that Vast's interruptible tier bills the license cost even on interrupted hours, so the 10 to 30% interruption loss is a charge already paid, not a refund, and an unsaved checkpoint means paying for compute you cannot recover [Ez2jsa33jFY @ 00:09:16]. HostingCompared with Natalie adds the duration trap: always add setup time, idle time, and a safety buffer to the offer's maximum rental window, because a cheap offer that expires before the checkpoint finishes is just a very affordable way to fail, and if one retry ruins the deadline, the lowest row may become the most expensive decision [cEAhnKuawL8 @ 00:01:02]. The rule that falls out: spot is for restartable work only, and anything with a deadline needs a host that can finish.

The quietest bleed is the bill that keeps running after the work stops. HostingCompared with Natalie spells out that stopping a RunPod pod releases the GPU but the volume disk keeps billing at the stopped rate of 20 cents per gigabyte per month, so 100 gigabytes is $20 a month, while on Vast storage keeps billing while the machine is online until you destroy the instance and delete any separate volume [OQpEhkeZZp4 @ 00:00:19]. Stopping also does not hold your hardware: hrithik verma tried restarting a stopped instance and was told it was CPU only because the GPU could not be started, so each fresh relaunch means waiting through Docker layers and Isaac Sim loading again while the meter runs [CkxWiz2Qzi8 @ 00:04:29]. GPU Battle found bandwidth eating 6 cents of a 17 cent Vast 4090 bill on the download alone [kvP__Lh53oM @ 00:01:44], and warns that downloading a 50 GB model on a GPU pod bills GPU hours the whole time, while an AI agent left unsupervised may park a pod on standby instead of terminating it and drain credits [WhTJ6B-YCmw @ 00:03:59]. Price the exit, the download, and the idle storage before you price the hour.

callout.title: Do Not Launch The Real Job Until The Host Passes
callout.body: Every practitioner who lost money on marketplace GPUs lost it on hosts that looked fine on the listing. Clear these four checks before committing a long run or walking away from a pod.
items: In the first two minutes, check the power limit, CPU, and download speed, and destroy the machine if anything is off [GPU Battle — dWC3n2Bn3r8 @ 00:05:34].

Set a minimum reliability score before sorting by price, because if one retry ruins the deadline the lowest row becomes the most expensive decision [HostingCompared with Natalie — cEAhnKuawL8 @ 00:00:40].
Route spot and interruptible pods only to restartable work, since about half of 17 spot attempts were kicked off before finishing [GPU Battle — kvP__Lh53oM @ 00:01:13].
Before leaving, back up, terminate the pod or destroy the instance, then open storage and delete orphaned network or Vast volumes [HostingCompared with Natalie — OQpEhkeZZp4 @ 00:01:19].

chapters.pull_quote: RunPod is the hour you don't have to baby sit, and vast.ai is the hour that costs less if nothing goes wrong. — Bryan Software (Ez2jsa33jFY @ 00:08:59)
action_checklist: Before launch, write down productive compute, paid idle time, storage lifetime, and expected transfer to price the whole job, not the hourly rate [HostingCompared with Natalie — _VqIjD7qiIg @ 00:00:00].
Prompt your renting agent to search by quality, not price: 99% plus reliability, 16 plus CPU cores, 800 plus megabytes per second, data center host preferred [GPU Battle — dWC3n2Bn3r8 @ 00:05:11].
Never trust one Vast host; run the same job on three hosts before committing real work [GPU Battle — 156XFkwFpwY @ 00:02:32].
Keep models on a network volume so you download once instead of billing GPU hours on every 50 GB pull [GPU Battle — WhTJ6B-YCmw @ 00:03:59].
Match the card to the job: a 3080 Ti, 3090, or 4090 for chat, images, voice, and 3D, saving H100s and B200s for big video models [GPU Battle — ymI6ZvqQNjQ @ 00:03:32].
When an offer leaves a fee unknown, price a minimum and maximum range instead of faking a precise total [HostingCompared with Natalie — _VqIjD7qiIg @ 00:02:44].

chapters.question_prompt: Where should GPU servers physically live, and what do colocation, power delivery, tiers, and IP or BGP connectivity really cost and require?
chapters.title: Colocation, Warehouses, and Data-Center Plumbing for GPU Operators
chapters.subtitle: Colo pricing for space, power, and cross-connects, a $25K/month warehouse GPU data center, homelab colo walkthroughs, a 36 MW facility tour, high-density colo, busways, RPPs, PDUs, and 1 MW HVDC racks, Uptime Tier 1-4 standards, ARIN registration, BGP over GRE without an ASN, and 44Net port forwarding
chapters.executive_summary: GPU operators choosing between colocation and a DIY warehouse face one dominant variable: power. Alec Glover ran 1,000 GPUs in a warehouse for about $25,000 a month, modeling $50 per kW-month against a colocation floor of $150 per kW-month billed on provisioned circuits, but admits the build was underspent and choked growth. IPTP Networks breaks colo quotes into six cost areas, pricing cross-connects at $500 to $1,500 install plus $100 to $300 monthly and remote hands at $150 to $350 an hour. Techno Tim found retail quotes of $350 to $900 a month and joined a split-cost rack instead. Lawrence Systems' Deft tour and Colovore stress redundancy and 20 kW density, while Null0 Labs shows GRE-tunneled BGP as a workaround when a building cannot get transit directly. Practitioners split on how much redundancy is worth paying for.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who priced real capacity lands on the same axis: power, not space. IPTP Networks calls power usually the largest variable on a colocation quote, billed either as a flat allocation of reserved capacity or by the meter on actual consumption, with redundant power adding roughly 15 to 20 percent; they flag that a standard server draws under half a kilowatt while a GPU server pulls 5 to 15 [3EnjHW-36GI @ 00:01:17]. Alec Glover, who ran a thousand GPUs, explains why that hurts: colos bill on power provisioned, so a GPU box needing a full 6 kW circuit pays for the whole circuit monthly whether it runs at 20 or 30 percent, and only larger deals unlock fixed price plus energy [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:01:30]. Colovore frames density as the second lever: an operator stuck in a decade-old facility capped at 4 kW per rack needs 10 racks and then 20 after growth, while a 20 kW-per-rack colo lets the same load fit in four 10 kW cabinets and grow vertically inside them [JMz8luHLVxc @ 00:00:20]. The shared baseline is simple: model kilowatts first, then rack units, because rack units alone will not explain why two quotes for the same footprint diverge.

Redundancy is the second point of agreement, and the vocabulary is the same whether the building is a Tier III colo or a warehouse. Alec Glover defines it as buying more units than you need, notated N+1 or N+2, and applies it bluntly to cooling: if the math says one air conditioner, you still buy two, because a single failure puts your SLAs at risk [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:07:34]. MEP BOOSTER gives the same arithmetic for Tier III design: if the load needs three units, install four, so one can fail while the remaining three carry full load, with dual power and cooling paths letting UPS maintenance, generator testing, or pump replacement happen while IT load keeps running [O0T9qQ1TuGU @ 00:15:24]. Gareth Knight pins Tier III at 99.982 percent uptime, under 1.6 hours of downtime a year, and positions it as the cost-versus-availability sweet spot below Tier IV [mNQb5B_voNw @ 00:03:51]. Data Center News adds the operator caveat everyone should internalize: simply building a Tier IV facility does not guarantee Tier IV uptime, because the site has to be consistently maintained and monitored, from temperature and humidity to power usage [8DzqbL0HKG0 @ 00:02:53]. Consensus: buy redundancy where a single failure kills customer uptime, and back it with monitoring.

The third shared conclusion is that connectivity and carrier presence decide whether a site is usable for paying customers. IPTP Networks notes that location and carrier ecosystem never appear in the rack rate, yet they determine what you can connect to and at what cost, from the number of ISPs and on-site internet exchanges to cloud on-ramps reached through cross-connects [3EnjHW-36GI @ 00:00:41]. Alec Glover treats the network as the next most important component after power: the building must support dedicated internet plans that let you run your own BGP router, and their warehouse ran a 10 Gbit primary backed by a 1 Gbit link, carrying about 100 servers per 10 gig [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:05:05]. Techno Tim saw the upside of carrier density firsthand at a Cologix site in downtown Minneapolis, where sub-millisecond pings came back over a site-to-site VPN because the home ISP also sat in that data center a few miles away [zbkqRPIUYAo @ 00:05:49]. Deft's team, touring with Lawrence Systems, warns that carriers sometimes run through the same manhole or conduit, so they build redundant fiber sides and route customers over diverse carriers so a single cut cannot take out both paths [gsN_CJJDy_o @ 00:12:21].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Start with the unit economics the operators actually paid. Alec Glover ran a thousand GPUs in a warehouse for almost three years at about $25,000 a month, and estimates a typical Tier III facility would have run three to five times that, a gap they say saved millions [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:00:00]. The math behind it: colocation has a hard time pricing below $150 per kilowatt per month, and Glover argues it has only gotten more expensive, while every DIY model they ran came in at $50 per kilowatt per month or less, because power that was not used was not paid for [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:01:49]. On top of power, IPTP Networks says connectivity is where colo quotes diverge most: every link to another provider or partner needs its own cross-connect, carrying an installation fee of typically $500 to $1,500 plus a monthly charge of around $100 to $300, so four cross-connects mean $2,000 to $6,000 upfront alone [3EnjHW-36GI @ 00:02:34]. The last recurring line is remote hands, the facility engineers doing reboots, drive swaps, and cable checks on your behalf, typically billed at $150 to $350 an hour with a one-hour minimum [3EnjHW-36GI @ 00:02:56]. Budget every one of these lines before comparing any warehouse lease.

For small footprints, the street move is to stop buying retail space and share a rack. Techno Tim called several data centers before colocating a homelab: one quoted half a cabinet, 24U, with 50 Mbps burstable to a gigabit, two switch ports, and 16 IPs for $900 a month plus a $4,500 one-time fee, and another offered 4U with 50 Mbps burst to 1 gigabit and one public IP for about $350 a month [zbkqRPIUYAo @ 00:00:50]. The workable option came from Will, who runs Plover Digital and rented a whole rack with friends to split the cost, which kept dropping as more people joined; Tim recommends that route outright [zbkqRPIUYAo @ 00:01:29]. IPTP Networks explains the structure behind it: top-tier facilities rarely sell less than a full rack, so 1U and partial cabinets typically come through a reseller or managed hosting provider rather than the data center itself [3EnjHW-36GI @ 00:00:56]. Some operators do slice inventory directly: Deft, on the Lawrence Systems tour, offers half cabinets and quarter-cabinet compartments to put two customers in the same physical space, secured with customer-changeable combination locks and optional fingerprint or card readers at the cabinet level [gsN_CJJDy_o @ 00:21:37]. The more tenants on the rack, the lower each share, which is the whole play.

Network plumbing is where operators cut the most cost with config rather than cash. Alec Glover first NATed public IPs to private addresses on machines, then switched to assigning public IPs directly on each server's interface, which made wiping a box, re-IPing it, and handing it to the next customer fast [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:06:26]. When a building cannot get BGP, Null0 Labs builds a plain GRE tunnel from the basement router to a router racked in a provider's data center, skipping IPSec because the tunnel only carries public transit, then splits the lent /24 into a /25 for the DC LAN and a /30 for the tunnel interfaces [Pr9psxw4Z_o @ 00:17:32]. The session starts on private ASN 64592; the upstream, running public AS900, strips the private ASN, sends only a default route, and filters inbound to the lent /24, so nobody on the internet sees the private ASN [Pr9psxw4Z_o @ 00:31:22]. Owning your own ASN is not stifling: Jeremy Cioara shows ARIN's autonomous system number at a $550 initial fee and $150 a year to maintain, while IPv4 blocks now come from a carrier, not ARIN, with authorization to advertise them over BGP [5WW8432TcR4 @ 00:03:15]. Underlay ISPs then become interchangeable plumbing.

callout.title: Field-Tested Shortcuts From the Cage and the Warehouse
callout.body: Small operational habits decide whether a remote rack is cheap to run or bleeds remote-hands hours and emergency drives across town.
items: Standardize identical servers and document serial numbers and disk positions so you can order parts before the drive to the facility [Techno Tim — zbkqRPIUYAo @ 00:02:20]

Lean on the colo parts room: Deft stocks common drive sizes because an 800 GB versus 960 GB mismatch can ruin your day, plus DAC cables and spare PDUs, with staff on site 24x7 to rack gear [Lawrence Systems — gsN_CJJDy_o @ 00:24:30]
Buy a PDU chassis whose behavior is set by a multi-pin cable, so one unit runs as a 20 amp 208 volt 3 kW PDU or a 17 kW monster by swapping only the cable [Lawrence Systems — gsN_CJJDy_o @ 00:27:05]
Use switched intelligent rack PDUs to power cycle a locked server remotely and track temperature and humidity exactly where GPUs draw intake air [Cakka | Cybersecurity — psGPevLhvpI @ 00:04:47]

sop_steps.title: Lock a BGP-capable underlay
sop_steps.action: Secure dedicated internet plans at the building with a primary and a backup link.
sop_steps.detail: Step one is finding a provider that offers BGP and dedicated internet at the bandwidth you need; Glover ran a 10 Gbit primary backed by a 1 Gbit link and carried about 100 servers on 10 gig [Alec Glover — TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:05:52]

sop_steps.title: Build the GRE tunnel to a transit-rich rack
sop_steps.action: Remove the default route, pin a static host route to the remote tunnel endpoint via the ISP, and bring up the tunnel.
sop_steps.detail: Delete the default route, add a static route to the remote router's public IP out of the ISP interface, then set tunnel source G1, the remote destination, and path MTU discovery; no IPSec is needed for public transit [Null0 Labs — Pr9psxw4Z_o @ 00:14:32]

sop_steps.title: Peer on a private ASN with a pull-up route
sop_steps.action: Run iBGP over the tunnel on a private ASN and nail the announced block to Null0.
sop_steps.detail: Configure router BGP 64592 with update-source tunnel 0, announce the /24, and add a static pull-up route to null 0 so the prefix appears in the BGP table; set next-hop-self toward the basement router [Null0 Labs — Pr9psxw4Z_o @ 00:26:29]

sop_steps.title: Cut over to a public ASN and your own block
sop_steps.action: Re-peer with the upstream on your public ASN and have them update prefix filters.
sop_steps.detail: After verifying block ownership with the upstream, the transit provider adds your new /22 to their inbound prefix list and outbound route map so it is announced to the internet instead of being filtered [Null0 Labs — Pr9psxw4Z_o @ 00:53:01]

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Alec Glover and the colocation sellers split hardest on who should own the building. Glover ran a thousand GPUs in a warehouse for almost three years at $25,000 a month and says a typical tier three data center would have cost three to five times as much [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:00:00]. His math: colos bill the full provisioned circuit, so a GPU server on a 6 kW circuit pays for all 6 kW whether it runs at 20% or 30%, and he says nobody will quote under $150 per kilowatt per month, while his own models landed at $50 or less because idle power was not billed [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:01:30]. IPTP Networks frames the same lever as a contract choice rather than a reason to leave: power can be a flat reserved allocation or metered on actual consumption, redundant power adds roughly 15 to 20%, and a GPU server draws 5 to 15 kW against under half a kilowatt for a standard box [3EnjHW-36GI @ 00:01:17]. Colovore argues the opposite fix, density: a legacy colo capping Don at 4 kW per rack forces ten racks, while Marty in a 20 kW-per-rack hall consolidates into four cabinets and grows vertically instead of buying more floor space [JMz8luHLVxc @ 00:00:20].

How much redundancy to buy is the second fault line. Glover argues the engineering in tier-rated buildings serves a valid purpose, but good enough is good enough and the savings from skipping functions can outweigh the drawbacks, then admits his own crew took it too far [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:00:27]. Gareth Knight pitches tier three as the sweet spot: N+1 on every critical component, concurrent maintainability, and 99.982% uptime, which he translates to less than 1.6 hours of downtime per year at reasonable cost compared with tier four [mNQb5B_voNw @ 00:03:51]. PCweb pushes the floor lower for small players, saying not every company needs tier four and that startups or small businesses can live with tier one or two, while enterprises where every second counts are stuck with three or four [0acbHqkQe80 @ 00:01:26]. Data Center News throws cold water on paying for the certificate alone: simply building a tier four facility does not guarantee tier four uptime, and without comprehensive monitoring even a tier four hall can go down unexpectedly, like a car with no dashboard [8DzqbL0HKG0 @ 00:02:53]. The split is plain: Glover buys redundancy only where customers feel it, the tier camp buys it as insurance, and the monitoring camp says the label is worthless without live telemetry.

On getting public IPs and routing into a GPU room, four playbooks compete. Glover went direct: buy dedicated internet plans that let you run your own BGP router, a 10 Gbit link backed by a 1 Gbit link, roughly 100 servers on the 10 gig, and his own public IPs that he eventually bound directly to server interfaces instead of NATing, so boxes could be wiped and re-handed to new customers [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:05:05]. Null0 Labs argues you do not need BGP at the building at all: run a plain GRE tunnel over a commodity ISP to a router in someone else's rack with real transit, peer with a private ASN that the upstream strips, and skip IPSec because the traffic is public anyway [Pr9psxw4Z_o @ 00:02:11]. Jeremy Cioara warns IPv4 no longer comes from ARIN, only from a carrier who authorizes you to advertise it, while an ASN runs $550 up front and $150 a year in maintenance [5WW8432TcR4 @ 00:03:15]. FEPLabs Radio shows the lightest option for ham operators stuck behind CGNAT on Starlink or a Verizon hotspot: a WireGuard tunnel to 44Net that lands a public 44.x address with no port forwards [ou57Rm_y3fs @ 00:08:04].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The loudest firsthand failure comes from Glover, who says the warehouse model was right but his execution was wrong: they cut so deep that scaling and growing the business became very difficult, and the build set the business back even while saving money [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:00:43]. A second utility feed from another substation was never an option because only one utility company served the area, so the failover layer big colos rely on simply did not exist [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:14:42]. Without generators, the only answer to customers during an outage is that power returns when the utility turns it back on, and cloud buyers already assume you sit in a real data center with backup power [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:13:34]. Lawrence Systems' Deft tour shows backup power failing even when you own it: generators run 500 kW to 3 MW each and must reach speed in about 16 seconds, but if the first unit latches onto the paralleling bus with a bad sine wave, the others refuse to sync and a site can end up with one of seven generators trying to carry the load [gsN_CJJDy_o @ 00:07:08].

Environmental shortcuts kill hardware quietly. Glover warns that running stock air conditioners strips moisture, and if humidity lands near 5% you risk a static shock that destroys a ton of hardware, so non-data-center units need bolt-on humidifiers and dehumidifiers [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:09:43]. His sharper warning is on free cooling: hardware coming out of old crypto-mining sites is absolutely destroyed after three years from wet, dirty air, with corrosion and salt buildup, so accelerated depreciation and lost resale value can outrun what skipping air conditioning saved [TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:10:48]. Cakka | Cybersecurity flags the electrical version of the same trap at GPU densities: a 120 kW rack at 480 V three-phase pulls 152 amps per phase versus 38 for a 30 kW rack, cable bundles choke trays and airflow, and a rack loading one phase heavily creates harmonic distortion and dangerous overheating at the upstream transformer [psGPevLhvpI @ 00:05:22]. Colovore shows the slow-motion version: Don, capped at 4 kW per rack, refreshes into power-hungry blade servers, fits even fewer per cabinet, and sprawls from ten to twenty cabinets that now all need managing [JMz8luHLVxc @ 00:01:15].

The recurring bill is where colo budgets leak. IPTP Networks puts every cross-connect at a $500 to $1,500 install plus $100 to $300 a month, so four cross-connects mean $2,000 to $6,000 upfront, and remote hands for reboots, drive swaps, and cable checks runs $150 to $350 an hour, usually with a one-hour minimum [3EnjHW-36GI @ 00:02:34]. Lawrence Systems' tour shows why on-site spares matter: crews drive two or three hours, discover the DAC cable or rack kit never shipped with a $40,000 storage array, and an 800 GB versus 960 GB SSD mismatch decides whether you have a good day or a bad one [gsN_CJJDy_o @ 00:24:01]. Techno Tim's countermeasure is to standardize every server's components and document serial numbers and disk positions so parts can be ordered before the drive downtown [zbkqRPIUYAo @ 00:02:20]. Beam Networks reports a software-side trap in a six-server colo rack: the Ceph cluster on shared 10 gig is extremely slow, adding disks slows the whole cluster for a while, RAM is at capacity, and storage sits at 66% with a warning, so Ceph is slated to be ripped out [4NmQ_0-0BC8 @ 00:04:21].
