callout.title: Four Checks Before You Sign a Colo Quote or Light Up a Warehouse
callout.body: Every item below is a loss, near-miss, or hidden bill a practitioner hit firsthand. Clear all four before committing GPUs to a room.
items: Price power both ways, provisioned versus metered, and refuse to pay monthly for a full 6 kW circuit your GPUs only use at 20% to 30% [Alec Glover — TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:01:30].
Read humidity the day you fire up non-data-center air conditioning; at 5% you risk a static shock that destroys a ton of hardware [Alec Glover — TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:09:43].
Count cross-connects into the quote before signing: four of them alone run $2,000 to $6,000 upfront before monthly charges [IPTP Networks — 3EnjHW-36GI @ 00:02:34].
Balance every high-density rack across all three phases before loading it, because one-phase draw overheats the upstream transformer [Cakka | Cybersecurity — psGPevLhvpI @ 00:05:22].

chapters.pull_quote: I ran a thousand GPUs in a warehouse for almost three years straight, and it only cost me $25,000 a month. Doing this in a typical tier three data center would cost you almost 3 to five times as much money. — Alec Glover (TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:00:00)
action_checklist: Call several facilities for quotes and compare rack space, bandwidth, IPs, and one-time fees line by line before committing to a shared or full rack (Techno Tim, zbkqRPIUYAo @ 00:00:50).
Ask every provider the same set of questions across all six cost areas so quotes become directly comparable (IPTP Networks, 3EnjHW-36GI @ 00:03:17).
Wire three-phase power from the start and put UPS between the transformer and the rack PDUs before calling a warehouse a data center (Alec Glover, TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:03:21).
Size air conditioning with many smaller units at N+1 or better so any single failure still leaves cooling running in every zone (Alec Glover, TZp1yBea0o4 @ 00:08:24).
If the building ISP will not offer BGP, run a GRE tunnel to your own router in a transit-rich rack elsewhere and peer from there (Null0 Labs, Pr9psxw4Z_o @ 01:02:09).
Open an ARIN account and point of contact now, and budget $550 for the initial ASN plus $150 a year in maintenance (Jeremy Cioara, 5WW8432TcR4 @ 00:03:15).

chapters.question_prompt: How do teams control cloud and AI spend, and when does bare metal or owning hardware beat hyperscaler bills?
chapters.title: FinOps and Repatriation: Controlling Cloud and AI Compute Spend
chapters.subtitle: AWS FinOps basics, CapEx vs OpEx and rightsizing, RI and savings-plan benchmarking, Amazon's internal cost lessons, FinOps+ at re:Invent, building a FinOps agent, agentic AI FinOps on Azure, AI budgets under tokenmaxxing, AI subscriptions vs owning an H100, $500 Epyc servers, and the $200 box vs $4,000 cloud bill
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from AWS, Vantage, ProsperOps, Kion and the FinOps Foundation converge on one sequence: hourly resource-level visibility, engineer ownership, policy-driven automation, then commitment and model-routing discipline. ProsperOps benchmarks average Effective Savings Rate at 10.5% against a 98th percentile near 40.5%, and its automation engine posts a 47% blended discount at over 98% coverage. Intellipaat pegs on-demand at two or three times committed rates. AI tokens now dominate the agenda: GenAI tops budget-overrun causes, FinOps X attendees spend 80% of their time on AI, and Vantage streams invocation logs because AWS billing lags seven to eight hours. The split comes on autonomy versus oversight and on repatriation: Nick Gioftsos champions a $200 box over a $4,000 cloud bill, while Caleb Writes Code finds a $200 subscription beats owning an H100.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator who spoke on this starts in the same place: you cannot cut what you cannot see. AWS With A Beer frames FinOps as a financial guard rail that forces engineering, finance and leadership into one room, and names lack of visibility, zombie instances, tangled pricing on data transfer and reserved instances, and organizational silos as the core leaks [6qqv9Ss3MaE @ 00:01:50]. Intellipaat pushes ownership down to the people launching the servers: finance experts will not fully understand ECS or Lambda versus EC2 choices, so developers must justify spend against business value and own the bill [7_L1_3-4kg8 @ 00:07:24]. Nathan Perry of the AWS OPTICS team describes how Amazon itself moved from monthly, account-level data to hourly, ARN-level grain using CUR and Data Exports, then democratized Cost Explorer to every team rather than hoarding it inside a central group [tPYmvdc5oE0 @ 00:02:17]. Rem at Vantage lays out the same sequence for AI spend: visibility, then allocation, then value measurement, then budgets and guardrails, in that order [1-lJfz3oQ2w @ 00:08:02]. The shared lesson is blunt. Get granular data into the hands of whoever controls the resource, attach a business owner to every dollar, and only then start cutting.

Rate optimization is the second point of agreement, and the numbers are loud. Intellipaat puts on-demand pricing at two or three times the cost of long-term commitment and argues a central team should own rate negotiation so engineers never touch it [7_L1_3-4kg8 @ 00:22:10]. ProsperOps' Erik Carlin pitches the logical extreme: software that buys and manages Reserved Instances and Savings Plans autonomously across more than $1B in annual compute, stating flatly that the platform does not provide recommendations, it acts [_ScBbR2FfCA @ 00:00:23]. Tatum Tummins of Kion makes the governance case for the same instinct, warning that a human review cycle of 30 to 60 days simply lets waste pile up while the ticket waits; the line is that policy becomes automation and automation becomes guardrails [NE8Ua2YVa6Q @ 00:06:12]. Nathan Perry keeps Amazon's automation policy- and threshold-triggered but logs every action and preserves human oversight, calling that balance crucial to building trust and driving adoption [tPYmvdc5oE0 @ 00:13:10]. The consensus position: commit to discounted rates centrally, encode waste definitions, snapshot retention, lights-off schedules and tagging rules as policy, and let machines execute faster than a monthly review meeting ever could, while keeping an audit trail humans can read.

The third shared conviction is that AI tokens have become the budget line that breaks plans. Jean of 451/S&P reports that GenAI was the top cause of budget overruns greater than 10%, and that FinOps X attendees now say 80% of their time goes to AI spend [N1u_6ENlZV4 @ 00:15:23]. Vantage's Ben adds that tracked spend across roughly 30 AI providers has tripled year-to-date, with customers commonly running 1,500 to 2,500 employees on Claude. In the Tokenmaxxing session, the Vantage team warns that leaderboards treating token burn as productivity are not sustainable because tokens cost money, and pushes cost per developer, cost per customer and cost per Linear ticket as the real yardsticks [1-lJfz3oQ2w @ 00:05:23]. Adam Richter of the AWS optics team reframes the job itself: FinOps is shifting from reading dashboards to asking whether ten large GPU instances are each idling at 10% when one at 100% would do [JqwiGt78aOI @ 00:07:58]. Intellipaat's unit math shows why per-unit thinking wins: a Lambda refactor lifts spend from $1,000 to $1,300 while users double from 1,000 to 2,000, pushing cost per customer below $1 [7_L1_3-4kg8 @ 00:35:30].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On commitments, ProsperOps publishes the scoreboard. Erik Carlin's example customer console shows 1,306 automated actions averaging more than 45 per day, near-perfect utilization, a 47% blended discount and over 98% coverage, with savings reported as incremental lifetime dollars net of the ProsperOps charge and allocated back by account, resource type or region through Intelligent Showback [_ScBbR2FfCA @ 00:01:08]. The ProsperOps benchmark across more than 1,400 data points, up to $2M per month in compute, sets the grading curve: average Effective Savings Rate is 10.5%, the 75th percentile sits in the low 20s and the 98th percentile hits about 40.5% [KW_LS_stgvc @ 00:03:35]. The same benchmark flags a savings-loss zone, mostly at smaller customers holding unused commitments, because it is actually possible with these instruments to lose money. Intellipaat's term rule is the street version: never buy a three-year plan for an application expected to last two, since one more year is completely wasted [7_L1_3-4kg8 @ 00:15:36]. On Azure, the FinOps Foundation demo overlays existing reservations and savings plans before acting on Advisor rightsizing, because shrinking a VM can leave an existing RI underutilized [b7TiwS4_Ytw @ 00:17:51].

Token spend gets its own toolkit. Vantage's demo wires OpenAI, Anthropic and Cursor billing into one view, drills from token usage into uncached input, cache writes, cache reads and output, then sets per-user budgets with anomaly alerts; joining application logs to Anthropic costs splits out agents that share a single API key [1-lJfz3oQ2w @ 00:24:06]. Ben at Vantage recommends Bedrock request metadata combined with virtual tags for attribution, and flags the billing-latency gap: AWS billing lags seven to eight hours while an engineer can blow up token usage inside an hour, so invocation logs should stream straight to the cost platform [N1u_6ENlZV4 @ 00:39:12]. Adam Richter's routing playbook uses Bedrock intelligent prompt routing, Opus to plan and Sonnet or Haiku to write code, with backoffs or sequential calls to dodge API throttling; input tokens run roughly four times cheaper than output, but input balloons over multi-turn chats [JqwiGt78aOI @ 00:18:04]. Hande Adiguzel treats the agent's context window as a budget to optimize rather than a limit, warning that handing an agent too many tools makes it slower, more expensive and likely to pick the wrong tool [b7TiwS4_Ytw @ 00:23:47].

Repatriation math is where the street gets specific. Caleb Writes Code runs the H100 numbers: a $200 monthly subscription over six years totals $14,400, buying an H100 costs about $30,000, and renting one from a neocloud at about $2.20 per hour for eight hours a day runs about $38,544 with weekends or $27,456 on weekdays only [SmYNK0kqaDI @ 00:01:20]. Sharing one card among four users shifts part of the math, since four subscriptions cost $57,600 while the H100 plus roughly $3,700 of electricity at $0.20 per kWh totals about $33,700, but Kimi K2 Thinking needs at least 14 H100s at full precision and a DGX H100 lands near $400K total cost of ownership, or 28 users to break even [SmYNK0kqaDI @ 00:05:08]. Craft Computing shows the cheap end: a Quanta T22HF two-node Epyc chassis with rails for $500, at a time when a single H11SSL board alone has climbed to $300 to $400 [JoqFD69bWLw @ 00:05:40]. Nick Gioftsos contrasts a $200 box against a client's $4,000 cloud bill for the same workload, and specs a roughly 15 W lab built on a Proxmox mini PC, a separate NAS, and a VLAN-segmented router and switch [rGnDq9evKng @ 00:00:00].

callout.title: Shortcuts operators pulled straight from their own demos
callout.body: Small configuration moves the speakers used to keep automation, agents and token budgets from biting back.
items: Instance Scheduler is tag-based, so warn developers who work weekends before lights-off schedules shut their boxes down [AWS Events — JqwiGt78aOI @ 00:14:19].
Start every FinOps agent read-only or human-in-the-loop, and confirm .gitignore hides access keys before the repo leaves the machine [AWS Events — JqwiGt78aOI @ 00:19:37].
Prompt compactors can raise output tokens, so measure the full bill before declaring a compression win [Vantage — 1-lJfz3oQ2w @ 00:30:15].

If a user cannot view cost in the Azure portal, neither can their agent, so sort cost-read permissions before enabling the ARM MCP Server cost toolsets via headers [FinOps Foundation — b7TiwS4_Ytw @ 00:26:56].

sop_steps.title: Drop to hourly, resource-level cost data
sop_steps.action: Enable CUR and Data Exports at hourly ARN grain and open Cost Explorer to every engineering team.
sop_steps.detail: Amazon moved off monthly account-level data, democratized Cost Explorer, and layered in tagging, Compute Optimizer, Cost Optimization Hub and Organizations [AWS Events — tPYmvdc5oE0 @ 00:02:17].

sop_steps.title: Set tiered, forecast-driven budgets
sop_steps.action: Build budgets by subscription or billing account, then app, then tags, with 50% and 75% thresholds on forecasted cost.
sop_steps.detail: Forecast-based budgets are more proactive and offset cost-data latency compared with alerts on actual spend [FinOps Foundation — b7TiwS4_Ytw @ 00:11:19].

sop_steps.title: Automate commitments and score them with ESR
sop_steps.action: Hand RI and Savings Plan management to automation and track Effective Savings Rate against the peer curve.
sop_steps.detail: Average ESR is 10.5%, the 75th percentile sits in the low 20s and the 98th percentile reaches about 40.5%, while unused commitments can push smaller accounts into a savings-loss zone [ProsperOps, a Flexera company — KW_LS_stgvc @ 00:03:35].

sop_steps.title: Instrument tokens in near real time
sop_steps.action: Stream model invocation logs into the cost platform, tag Bedrock requests, and set per-user budgets with anomaly alerts.
sop_steps.detail: AWS billing lags seven to eight hours while an engineer can blow up token usage within an hour, so invocation logs plus Bedrock request metadata and virtual tags close the gap [Vantage — N1u_6ENlZV4 @ 00:39:12].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The build-versus-buy fight is the sharpest split in the room. Jean of 451/S&P, speaking on Vantage, tracks a repeating arc: shops start with a first-party tool, try to roll their own, then end up buying a capable third-party platform [N1u_6ENlZV4 @ 00:06:38]. Nathan Perry of the AWS OPTICS team, after 11 years inside Amazon, goes further and labels the early custom-build confidence 'Dunning Kruger', a lesson the Amazon team paid to learn [tPYmvdc5oE0 @ 00:19:27]. Adam Richter, also on the optics team, does not ban building. Richter wires up a live FinOps agent on camera with Kiro CLI, Strands and the Billing and Cost Management MCP, but warns that the moment you build, you own support and security yourself [JqwiGt78aOI @ 00:09:22]. ProsperOps takes the opposite pole from every dashboard vendor: Erik Carlin states flatly that the platform does not provide recommendations, it acts, with ProsperBot buying and reshaping RIs and Savings Plans autonomously across more than $1B in annual compute [_ScBbR2FfCA @ 00:00:23]. The operator choice is three-way: buy visibility, build an agent you will maintain forever, or hand the commitment portfolio to an autonomous engine and judge it purely on incremental savings net of its own charge.

How fast automation should fire is the second fault line. Tatum Tummins of Kion, who spent 7.5 years running FinOps in healthcare, argues that a human review cycle of 30 to 60 days simply lets waste accrue in the meantime, and pushes policy straight into automated guardrails: orphan definitions, snapshot retention, lights-off for dev and sandbox, and enforced tag key-value pairs [NE8Ua2YVa6Q @ 00:06:12]. Nathan Perry runs Amazon's own estate with a counterweight, keeping policy- and threshold-triggered automation paired with human oversight and logging every single action, calling that balance crucial to building trust and driving adoption [tPYmvdc5oE0 @ 00:13:10]. Adam Richter sits even further toward caution for agents, preferring to start read-only or human-in-the-loop before granting any write access [JqwiGt78aOI @ 00:19:37]. The Microsoft team of Vikram Desai and Hande Adiguzel lands on a hybrid: the GitHub Copilot CLI agent pulls Advisor usage and rate recommendations, overlays existing RIs and savings plans, then ships the change as a Terraform pull request for human approval [b7TiwS4_Ytw @ 00:20:35]. Kion's fast lane looks like an AI-written Cloud Custodian policy that snapshots unattached EBS volumes older than 7 days and then deletes them; the Microsoft lane routes every change through a reviewer first.

The repatriation debate splits cleanly between cloud economics and owned iron. CloudExpert Solutions frames CapEx as the losing bet: $2M on servers over five years, traffic drops by year three, the hardware is outdated by year five, and you carry the full risk, while OpEx scales from 10 to 50 to 5 servers with 'zero waste' [dpje7Qql0SU @ 00:02:47]. Nick Gioftsos, a systems and cloud engineer working in Azure and Microsoft 365, opens with the counter-punch: a $200 box doing the same workload as a client's $4,000 cloud bill, with the team sitting idle for three hours during a regional hiccup, and a warning that cloud-only engineers are building careers on rented land [rGnDq9evKng @ 00:00:00]. Caleb Writes Code runs the GPU version of the same math and lands on the rental side: $200 a month in subscriptions for six years totals $14,400 against roughly $30,000 for one H100, so 'the math doesn't really work in our favor' for owning [SmYNK0kqaDI @ 00:01:03]. Hostrunway pitches the middle path: dedicated bare metal with H100, H200 and B300 GPUs, no hypervisor, no noisy neighbors, billed month-to-month with no lock-in [Auj5NAlVFVk @ 00:02:13]. Even Gioftsos concedes the cloud isn't going away.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Commitments are where operators bleed fastest. ProsperOps built a benchmark of more than 1,400 data points covering up to $2M a month in compute spend, and it maps a savings-loss zone where unused commitments turn into a net loss: 'it's actually possible with these instruments to lose money', with that zone dominated by smaller customers [KW_LS_stgvc @ 00:01:58]. Right above it sits a no-savings zone where commitments go unused at spend levels up to roughly $250K to $500K a month, and the average Effective Savings Rate across the whole set is only 10.5%, against the low 20s at the 75th percentile and about 40.5% at the 98th [KW_LS_stgvc @ 00:03:35]. Intellipaat's instructor gives the simplest version of the trap: buy a three-year plan for an app predicted to live two years and 'one more year would be completely wasted' [7_L1_3-4kg8 @ 00:15:36]. The Microsoft demo exposes the collision between rate and usage optimization: right-sizing a VM can leave an existing reservation underutilized, which is why the Copilot agent overlays current RIs and savings plans on top of Advisor recommendations before proposing any change [b7TiwS4_Ytw @ 00:17:51]. Rate wins and usage wins fight each other unless one workflow sees both at the same time.

AI spend breaks the old monthly-close rhythm. Ben of Vantage and Jean of 451/S&P both flag the latency gap: AWS billing lags 7 to 8 hours, while an engineer can blow up token usage inside an hour, so the fix is streaming invocation logs straight into the cost platform, and both agree there is still room for improvement [N1u_6ENlZV4 @ 00:39:12]. Tokenmaxxing creates its own perverse incentives: Vantage's session on AI budgets warns that smaller PRs drive tokens-per-PR down without improving cost-per-feature, and prompt reuse inflates cache-hit ratios, so any single KPI gets gamed and teams must track many of them [1-lJfz3oQ2w @ 00:14:57]. The same session reports that prompt compactors can raise output tokens, the opposite of what an operator buys them for [1-lJfz3oQ2w @ 00:30:15]. Adam Richter adds the math behind that trap: input tokens run about four times cheaper than output, but input balloons as multi-turn chats carry history forward, and the consensus-plus-judge agent pattern that cuts hallucination costs more to run [JqwiGt78aOI @ 00:18:04]. Vantage's rule is to decide the over-budget action, downgrade the model or stop usage, before the spike hits, while protecting end users in application AI.

Repatriating to owned hardware trades the cloud bill for a new set of failure points. Craft Computing bought two AMD Epyc nodes in a Quanta T22HF chassis for $500 including rails, then hit a wall: one proprietary U.2 power cable, zero vendor documentation for a 2018 server, no POST after about 20 minutes, and a BMC that appears cloud-connected to Quanta, requiring a license and active subscription to manage your own local hardware [JoqFD69bWLw @ 00:15:33]. Quanta's answer was that it does not recommend CPUs not designed for the platform and cannot provide relevant documentation, leaving the fix to crowdsourcing [JoqFD69bWLw @ 00:19:39]. Caleb Writes Code finds the GPU version of the same trap: Kimi K2 Thinking needs at least 14 H100s at full precision, a DGX H100 runs $285K to $300K, about $400K total cost of ownership, and needs 28 users to break even [SmYNK0kqaDI @ 00:05:08]. Even then, the 140 GB left for KV cache yields roughly 80,000 tokens, about 2,850 per person. Nick Gioftsos names the cloud-side trap as the virtual taximeter: fear of a $400 bill drives a terraform destroy after 45 minutes, so day-90 problems like a full /var, expired certificates and memory leaks never surface [rGnDq9evKng @ 00:03:58].

Before buying used servers, verify the BMC is not locked behind a vendor cloud license and that documentation exists for the platform [Craft Computing — JoqFD69bWLw @ 00:15:33].

chapters.question_prompt: How do neoclouds make money, and how do teams broker and schedule GPU jobs across multiple clouds and clusters?
chapters.title: Neocloud Economics and Multi-Cloud GPU Brokerage
chapters.subtitle: Single-H100 neocloud unit economics, CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, Lambda, and Fluidstack, GPUaaS, startups leaving AWS and Azure for bare metal, debt-financed buildouts from the telecom bust, SkyPilot as an intercloud broker at Meta scale, unscheduled-GPU diagnosis, gang scheduling and preemption, spot-checkpoint math, CoreWeave SUNK, Modelplane, and multi-node fine-tuning on Nebius
chapters.executive_summary: Neocloud operators and multi-cloud brokers converge on one law: idle or stalled GPUs bleed money, so utilization, scheduling and portability decide who survives. Caleb Writes Code models a $25K H100 rented at $2.30/hr returning a 28% CAGR only at full utilization, with broad stocks winning below roughly 55%. Neoclouds list GPUs at roughly half to two-thirds of hyperscaler prices and up to 30-50% cheaper on contract, while SkyPilot's broker finds up to 3x on-demand and 9x spot price spreads across zones. Street mechanics center on queues with priority preemption, checkpointed spot runs saved near a 34-minute interval, and one YAML spec that fails over across clouds. Disagreement persists over provider picks, Slurm versus Kubernetes, and whether neocloud debt echoes the telecom bust, where a NY-LA circuit collapsed from $1.8M to under $150K a year.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator in this chapter starts from the same brutal arithmetic: a GPU only earns while it is busy. Caleb Writes Code prices a single H100 at $25K plus $5K opex, gives it roughly 4 years of useful life, and shows that renting it at $2.30/hr yields about $55 a day, near $20K a year and about $80K over four years, which works out to a 28% CAGR only at 100% utilization; at or below roughly 55% utilization, broad stocks beat the neocloud outright [9u2hCf8FlW0 @ 00:01:22]. The gpuMaster frames the same pain from the renter side: stalled GPUs still bill, and large-scale GPU workloads are 'far less forgiving' [_tV0Elv_jIk @ 00:01:29]. Codemia puts a dollar figure on scheduler quality for a 10,000-GPU fleet: default Kubernetes lands near 45% utilization, a workload-aware design reaches about 85%, and that gap is worth roughly $150k per day [a_zou7QahAo @ 00:04:38]. The Code Notebook compresses the whole consensus into one line, 'The cheapest GPU is one that is switched off,' backed by a scale-to-zero simulation that cut 24 GPU-hours to 4.04, an 83% reduction, at a cost of 3.9 cold starts per day lasting 60 seconds each [IZtzUfhm8LU @ 00:12:17].

The second point of agreement is that neoclouds win on price and workload fit, not on breadth of services. Cloud Computing Insider defines a neocloud as an AI-first, GPU-centric provider and argues that hyperscalers were built for all IT, while neoclouds were built for the compute, networking and storage patterns modern AI needs, and hyperscalers charge more for AI because they run it less efficiently [mAgWtefgeP8 @ 00:01:02]. Romil Bhardwaj of SkyPilot, speaking at TMLS, lists the neocloud edge as instant self-serve capacity, 3.2TB/s InfiniBand, top SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX tiers, and pricing up to 30 to 50% cheaper depending on contract length, while warning that the long tail of neoclouds runs 2 to 3x cheaper but less reliable [_oWJ0t-RW7o @ 00:06:30]. The Code Notebook, working from vendor figures dated October 2026, pegs neocloud GPU list prices at roughly one-half to two-thirds of big-cloud rates [IZtzUfhm8LU @ 00:05:29]. Caleb Writes Code, whose own model assumes a market rate of $1 to $5 per hour across CoreWeave, Runpod, Vultr and Thunder Compute, adds the hard corollary: neoclouds are heavily commoditized, customers typically look for the cheapest pricing, and any operator who charges a premium watches utilization fall [9u2hCf8FlW0 @ 00:01:37].

The third consensus is that no serious buyer stays on one provider. Zhanghao Wu and Kevin Mingtarja of SkyPilot open their frontier-capabilities talk by pointing to Meta signing multi-billion-dollar deals with CoreWeave and Nebius and give three reasons to run multi-provider: capacity, cost, and no single point of failure [uwLkrJb5pEA @ 00:01:47]. Romil Bhardwaj, presenting at CNCF, traces OpenAI's move from Microsoft exclusivity to Oracle, CoreWeave and GCP [-czZES1U_Us @ 00:00:49]. The USENIX NSDI '23 SkyPilot team makes the economic case for brokerage: silos reduce availability and leverage, a single-cloud business is more vulnerable to large-scale outages, and it has lower negotiation leverage to get a better deal because 'choice is power' [3Edw88b1bRg @ 00:01:22]. Their broker example routes SGX workloads to Azure, TPU training to GCP and Inferentia inference to AWS. Cloud Computing Insider expects the end state to be a hybrid, heterogeneous mix, telling buyers that a best-of-breed play is going to be complex and heterogeneous, and that if they shortlist two providers it is probably Nebius and CoreWeave, while disclaiming any single-provider recommendation [mAgWtefgeP8 @ 00:13:14]. The prerequisite all of them share is a portability layer that lets workloads move when prices, quotas or availability shift.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On the supply side, the build math gets heavier fast. Caleb Writes Code notes that a GPT-3-class model needs more than 350GB of VRAM, so a serious customer needs at least 8 H100s, which puts the minimum rentable unit at $250K: $200K for cards and $50K opex; eBay cards are risky, and supplier relationships act as the moat [9u2hCf8FlW0 @ 00:03:59]. Scaling is non-linear: efficiency drops to 77% at 8 GPUs under model parallelism and 74% at 512 per an NVIDIA paper, fragmented nodes create bottlenecks, and scheduling turns into Tetris. CUDA and ROCm workloads are not interchangeable, so a mixed fleet carries heterogeneity risk. On financing, Caleb Writes Code points out that resale value stays near purchase price, which enables asset-backed loans, while contracts trade a discount for flexibility [9u2hCf8FlW0 @ 00:13:55]. Codemia sizes a 10,000-GPU fleet at about $400M across 1,250 hosts in 32 racks, with cards renting at $20 to $40 per hour [a_zou7QahAo @ 00:03:35]. Reliability becomes a sales weapon: Deok Filho of CoreWeave cites Meta's figure of roughly 8 hours between interruptions per 1,000 GPUs and claims CoreWeave runs 70 to 80 hours for an equivalent job size [vdP0fhqpYZs @ 00:06:03].

On the buy side, The Code Notebook lays out the pricing ladder: flex start runs about half price, commitments go down to about 45%, and spot goes down to about 9% [IZtzUfhm8LU @ 00:06:06]. The commitment rule is simple: utilization must exceed 1 minus the discount. With $10 on-demand, a $4.50 commit costs $5 per used hour at 90% busy but $45 per used hour at 10% busy, hence 'Never commit to your peak.' Spot carries a different tax: AWS gives 2 minutes of warning and Azure gives 30 seconds. In a 2,000-run simulation of a 100-hour job with interruptions every 8 hours, 6-minute restarts, 72-second saves and a 70% discount, never saving produced 2,203,564 hours, saving every 30 minutes finished in 109 hours at a cost of 32.6 against 100 on-demand, and saving every 30 seconds took 345 hours at 103.5. The optimal save interval, the square root of 2 times MTBI times save cost, lands near 34 minutes [IZtzUfhm8LU @ 00:10:20]. The USENIX SkyPilot team measured the spread that makes brokering pay: up to 3x on on-demand pricing and up to 9x on spot across zones [3Edw88b1bRg @ 00:07:21]. Codemia's scheduler polls for spot reclaim every 5 seconds against the 2-minute warning [a_zou7QahAo @ 00:29:02].

The brokerage layer itself is mostly scheduling and provisioning plumbing. SkyPilot's Zhanghao Wu and Kevin Mingtarja run `sky launch --gpus B200` for a dev box, bump `num_nodes 16` to scale out, and use `sky jobs launch` so a GPU failure, node maintenance, quota reclamation or spot preemption is recovered hands-free; in their demo the optimizer picked the cheapest option, an already-provisioned CoreWeave H100 node [uwLkrJb5pEA @ 00:08:31]. At Meta FAIR, Lucca Bertoncini found a 10-step setup lost about 90% of users by step 2 and 98% by the end, and 2FA on every cluster drove adoption to 0%, so the team shipped a single binary that writes the configuration and holds SSH/ET tunnels in tmux with 2FA done once, across clusters of roughly 20K GPUs each [Pas2NE76220 @ 00:05:54]. Seung Jin Yang of SkyPilot replaces spreadsheets and node taints with a real queue, priority preemption backed by checkpoints, Slack alerts on preemption, and quota borrowing that lets a team grab 256 GPUs idling in another team's queue [tb-Yg8PNXT4 @ 00:05:02]. Alex from Nebius shows SkyPilot task definitions running 3 to 4x shorter than the Kubernetes equivalent, driving a 2-node, 16-H100 Llama 3.1 fine-tune with TorchTune [QLSYI5Ali8Y @ 00:02:24].

callout.title: What The Brokers Do Before Spending A Dollar
callout.body: The operators who win on GPU arbitrage test before they sign, request capabilities instead of clusters, and price work rather than sticker hours.
items: Run your own end-to-end workload in a roughly week-long POC before signing, and use multicloud optionality as negotiating leverage [Toronto Machine Learning Society (TMLS) — _oWJ0t-RW7o @ 00:07:47].
Never build a plan around a chip that is only announced, and always test your own workload before you sign anything [The Code Notebook — IZtzUfhm8LU @ 00:04:26].

Request intent, not hardware: a `network_tier: best` field gets translated to EFA or GPUDirect per cloud, with raw pod specs kept as an escape hatch [CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation] — -czZES1U_Us @ 00:12:15].

Declare requirements, not clusters: the deployment asked for 8 GPUs with at least 140GB VRAM on vLLM, never named the cluster, and placed 2 replicas across AWS and CoreWeave [Modelplane — Wq9Ov_jlxlM @ 00:03:54].

sop_steps.action: Commit only the capacity you will keep busier than the break-even line.

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is whether to own GPUs or arbitrage other people's capacity. Caleb Writes Code runs the owner math cold: a $25,000 H100 plus $5,000 opex, a four-year life, and $2.30 per hour yielding roughly $55 a day, about $20,000 a year and $80,000 over the card's life, a 28% CAGR only at 100% utilization [9u2hCf8FlW0 @ 00:00:50]. Drop to roughly 55% utilization and broad stocks beat the neocloud, and because the market is commoditized, any premium price simply bleeds utilization [9u2hCf8FlW0 @ 00:01:22]. Romil Bhardwaj attacks from the buyer side: the long tail of neoclouds runs two to three times cheaper but is less reliable, and neoclouds can land 30 to 50% cheaper depending on how long a contract you sign [_oWJ0t-RW7o @ 00:06:30]. Cloud Computing Insider frames the same gap structurally, arguing hyperscalers charge more for AI because they were built for all IT and are less efficient at it [mAgWtefgeP8 @ 00:01:49]. The owner needs full racks and steady renters; the broker profits when that owner's margin collapses under competition. Both camps agree price is the battlefield, but they sit on opposite sides of the same spread, and an operator has to decide which side of that spread pays the bills before buying a single card.

The second fight is concentration versus brokerage. Cloud Computing Insider will name names, saying if you look at two providers it is probably Nebius and CoreWeave, with CoreWeave as the gold standard, yet the same speaker refuses to back a single provider and warns that a best-of-breed play will be complex and heterogeneous [mAgWtefgeP8 @ 00:13:14]. CoreWeave's Deok Filho pushes concentration hard: Meta reports about eight hours between interruptions per 1,000 GPUs, CoreWeave claims 70 to 80 hours for an equivalent job size, and the pitch closes with 'It just will run better on us' [vdP0fhqpYZs @ 00:06:03]. The Sky Computing team at USENIX argues the opposite, that silos cut availability and negotiation leverage because choice is power, and that clouds will never commoditize themselves through standardization, so a broker must sit on top [3Edw88b1bRg @ 00:01:22]. Modelplane adds a sharper twist: the multi-cloud layer is too important to be proprietary, and clusters should be treated as one fleet where a deployment never names the cluster at all [Wq9Ov_jlxlM @ 00:02:46]. Single-vendor depth buys reliability numbers and integrated tooling; brokerage buys leverage and failover. Neither camp disputes the other's data, only which risk an operator should eat.

The third split is how to buy time on the iron. Caleb Writes Code treats contracts as a plain trade of discount for flexibility [9u2hCf8FlW0 @ 00:11:30]. The Code Notebook maps the buyer's full ladder: flex start at about half price, commitments down to about 45%, spot down to about 9%, and a hard rule that a commitment only wins when utilization exceeds one minus the discount, summed up as 'Never commit to your peak' [IZtzUfhm8LU @ 00:07:52]. The USENIX SkyPilot team bets on the spread instead, measuring up to three times difference in on-demand pricing and up to nine times in spot pricing across zones, then routing jobs with an ILP solver that minimizes total cost or time [3Edw88b1bRg @ 00:07:21]. Underneath the pricing sits a cluster-manager argument. Romil Bhardwaj says Slurm hits isolation and serving limits, Kubernetes brings a steep learning curve with no SSH and no gang scheduling, and raw VMs dump key management and manual orchestration on the team, so the recommendation is managed Kubernetes plus VMs [_oWJ0t-RW7o @ 00:11:41]. CoreWeave answers by running Slurm on Kubernetes through SUNK, while Meta FAIR still flags schedulers stacked on schedulers as an open problem. Each answer reshapes how much of the discount actually reaches the bottom line.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive trap is cheap spot capacity run without discipline. The Code Notebook simulated a 100-hour job with interruptions every eight hours, a six-minute restart, 72 seconds per save, 2,000 runs, and a 70% discount: never saving stretched the job to 2,203,564 hours, saving every 30 minutes finished in 109 hours at a cost of 32.6 against 100 on-demand, and saving every 30 seconds ballooned to 345 hours at 103.5 [IZtzUfhm8LU @ 00:09:58]. Their verdict is that spot without checkpoints is not cheap, saving too often costs more than not using spot at all, and the optimal interval is the square root of two times mean time between interruptions times save cost, about 34 minutes [IZtzUfhm8LU @ 00:10:20]. The same speaker notes the warning windows are brutal: AWS gives two minutes and Azure gives 30 seconds. Codemia's scheduler design polls the two-minute reclaim notice every five seconds and tells operators to give each job a random offset so checkpoint timers do not line up, because correlated failures are where these systems break [a_zou7QahAo @ 00:31:58]. SkyPilot's managed jobs layer pitches hands-free recovery from GPU failure, node maintenance, quota reclamation, and spot preemption so nobody gets paged at 3:00 a.m. [uwLkrJb5pEA @ 00:08:31].

The second trap is paying for GPUs that are not doing work. The gpuMaster's core warning is that stalled GPUs still bill, and that large-scale GPU workloads are far less forgiving [_tV0Elv_jIk @ 00:01:29]. Caleb Writes Code measured the scaling tax: efficiency drops to 77% at eight GPUs under model parallelism and 74% at 512, and fragmented nodes turn scheduling into Tetris [9u2hCf8FlW0 @ 00:05:04]. Seung Jin Yang of SkyPilot debugged the failures researchers actually hit when they ask why their job is not scheduled: fragmentation, rogue taints left by agents, a request for 128 CPUs on nodes with only about 126.32 allocatable that shows up as blocked, and quota oversubscription where 12 GPUs are promised against 8, which, in their words, can happen in practice [tb-Yg8PNXT4 @ 00:13:27]. Codemia prices the gap: default Kubernetes gets about 45% utilization, a workload-aware design about 85%, a spread worth roughly $150,000 per day on a 10,000-GPU fleet [a_zou7QahAo @ 00:04:38]. The same speaker caps defragmentation at 5% per hour, because the cure has to stay cheaper than the disease. Every one of these leaks lands as billed GPU hours with zero training progress behind them.

The third trap is the balance sheet. Tulipnomics walks through the telecom bust as a template: Lucent promised $6.7 billion in customer credit by September 2000, with Nortel and Cisco running similar programs, summed up as the seller lending the buyer the money to buy the seller's own products [71yv5MpdX1s @ 00:02:24]. When capacity flooded in, a New York to Los Angeles circuit fell from $1.8 million a year to under $150,000, telecom made up over half of 2002 bond defaults with 21 cents of recovery, and the same channel now counts roughly $36 billion of CoreWeave debt plus Moody's tally of $1.2 trillion in lease commitments, $820 billion not yet started [71yv5MpdX1s @ 00:09:54]. theCUBE flags the operator-level exposure: a 2024 net loss of $863.4 million, NVIDIA dependence, and over 60% of revenue from Microsoft, with the warning that sustaining profitability is going to be another challenge [VjfoLNKgo3A @ 00:03:51]. Caleb Writes Code offers the counterweight, noting that GPU resale value stays near purchase price, which enables asset-backed loans [9u2hCf8FlW0 @ 00:13:55]. Tulipnomics' own coda cuts both ways: the cable was never the problem, but new owners bought the networks for a fraction of what they cost to build, and the banks lost money on the fiber.

chapters.question_prompt: How do I slice and share GPUs safely across multiple tenants on Kubernetes so expensive capacity isn't idle?
chapters.title: Multi-Tenant GPU Sharing on Kubernetes
chapters.subtitle: NVIDIA GPU Operator deployment, time-slicing replicas, MIG spatial partitioning and MIG-backed vGPU, MPS and Ray sharing, memory-safe dynamic time-slicing, vCluster, Open WebUI, OpenShift AI with KAI, Run:ai team sharing, HAMi vendor-neutral observability, DRA sharing-strategy benchmarks, and transparent GPU pod checkpointing
chapters.executive_summary: Operators sharing GPUs on Kubernetes converge on one stack: the NVIDIA GPU operator for drivers, device plugin and DCGM, then a sharing layer chosen by workload. Time slicing advertises phantom replicas (Rafay flips an A10 between 2, 6 and 10 via a node label; vCluster runs 4 replicas on an RTX 5070 Ti) but gives no memory isolation, and Kubex watched a leaky classifier OOM-kill a neighbor LLM on a 24 GB L4. MIG carves an A100 into up to seven 1g.5gb slices with fault isolation, at the cost of static sizing. MPS, benchmarked by Klues and Chen, roughly doubles light-load utilization and, capped at 10% for low-priority work, holds near-dedicated performance. The split is throughput versus latency: Emmanuel Corels measured A100 throughput rising from 0.76 to 1.0 requests/s under MIG while time sharing kept mean latency lower.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who actually ships shared GPUs starts from the same foundation: the NVIDIA GPU operator. Techi Nik frames its job bluntly — it detects GPU nodes, installs the NVIDIA drivers, manages GPU resources, and skips any node without a card, so mixed clusters stay clean [f-FKoMHqRoI @ 00:00:35]. Saiyam of vCluster lists the full payload the operator drops onto each GPU node: CUDA drivers, the container runtime, the device plugin, metrics, and GPU feature discovery [sXpJ4vSc-cM @ 00:31:46]. That discovery layer is what surfaces sharing to the Kubernetes scheduler. On Rafay's MKS cluster, the operator stamps nvidia.com labels onto the GPU node reporting GPU present true, an NVIDIA A10, a physical count of 1, and a time-slicing strategy with 10 replicas, so a single card shows up to the scheduler as ten [n-O8p7y9Z5A @ 00:00:44]. Jitesh Powankar calls enablement straightforward: install the operator, configure node policies, and once configured Kubernetes automatically discovers the new slices and reports them like CPU or memory [Ul1dZowvKvE @ 00:03:58]. The operator consensus is that nobody hand-rolls drivers and device plugins per node; the operator owns that layer, and every sharing strategy — time slicing, MIG, or fractional scheduling — is expressed as a label, a config, or an annotation that the operator and scheduler reconcile.

The business case is idle silicon. Jitesh Powankar puts numbers on it: a pod that requests a whole card may use only 20 to 30 percent, leaving 70 percent idle while other pods queue — like booking a whole 50-seat bus for one passenger [Ul1dZowvKvE @ 00:00:34]. The Code Architect drills into the hardware reason: a light task occupies about 10 percent of the streaming multiprocessors and the other 90 percent sit idle, because separate CUDA contexts cannot run concurrently, and an H100 is far more than a 256M-parameter model needs [TwICQ_zP8Ys @ 00:02:40]. Saiyam states the default outcome without a sharing layer: one pod takes the entire GPU, and no one else can use it until it releases it [sXpJ4vSc-cM @ 00:34:26]. The DevOps & AI Toolkit host hit that wall live on GKE: after llama 2 grabbed the single GPU with a limit of nvidia.com/gpu equal to 1, the second model sat Pending with no available GPUs, and buying another node only makes sense when the first is at full capacity — otherwise it is a waste of money [zuRKdveFuZ4 @ 00:08:47]. The shared conclusion: the default one-pod-one-card model burns budget, and the arbitrage is packing multiple tenants onto hardware you already pay for.

There is also broad agreement that no single mechanism wins; the mechanism has to match the workload. Kevin Klues frames it as space versus time partitioning, a fundamental inherent trade-off: MIG delivers full fault isolation and memory-bandwidth QoS but fixed partition sizes, while MPS offers flexible sizes with limited isolation that does not suit multi-tenancy [nOgxv_R13Dg @ 00:05:00]. Emmanuel Corels Academy describes the same split from the tenant's seat: time sharing lends idle capacity to other jobs but jobs compete when both are busy, whereas MIG gives isolated slices with no borrowing, so reserved capacity can sit idle [sRtvITK_o8I @ 00:00:52]. The Code Architect compresses it into a rule: time slicing for bursty heterogeneous workloads, MPS for trusted and predictable ones, MIG for absolute isolation [TwICQ_zP8Ys @ 00:08:03]. Core Concept Learning shows what that looks like across three teams on Run:ai: inference GPUs split into up to seven MIG instances, notebooks on Run:ai fractional GPUs, and large training kept on full GPUs, with the exam-grade advice to match the mechanism to the workload and each team's guarantee [56JbSXiXhhE @ 00:01:37]. Hardware gates the menu: The Code Architect notes MIG requires Ampere or newer, and Emmanuel Corels Academy flags the L4 as lacking MIG entirely.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Time slicing is a config-and-label game. Rafay's cluster runs a GPU blueprint (V2) mapped to an NVIDIA GPU operator add-on carrying time-slice configs for 2, 6 and 10 replicas; the engineer edits the node's nvidia.com label to profile six, saves it, and the operator reconciles 10 replicas down to 6 in a few seconds, then flips back to 10 when more applications need to land [n-O8p7y9Z5A @ 00:02:13]. The vCluster step-by-step runs the host side with GPU operator 25.3.0 and 4 replicas: create the time-slicing config, patch it, then describe the node to confirm 1 GPU advertising 4 replicas; inside each tenant vCluster with nodes enabled, reinstall the operator with the toolkit and driver disabled, reapply and re-patch, and expect a node refresh before 4 replicas appear [KzJvhbdgvl8 @ 00:01:27]. On GKE, Saiyam simply sets time-sharing with max shared clients per GPU at five on a single Tesla T4 and notes GKE automatically handles the operator install [sXpJ4vSc-cM @ 00:44:18]. Under the hood, Kevin Klues explains the device-plugin model: nvidia.com/gpu, GFD labels, a per-node replicas config such as 3, and a .shared suffix on the advertised resource [nOgxv_R13Dg @ 00:09:27]. Skip the replicas, the vCluster demo warns, and pods fail to schedule.

MIG is spatial and declarative. Rafay's upstream cluster shows a single A100 labeled MIG capable true; the blueprint layers an add-on setting the MIG single strategy, and because every partition is the same size the operator slices to the maximum the card supports — seven GPUs reported as GPU 0 through 6 [YoZoDn_Fvq0 @ 00:01:58]. A five-replica test app scheduled against all-1g.5gb nodes comes up with identical GPU UUIDs but distinct MIG UUIDs, which is the verification check. The DevOps & AI Toolkit host recreated a GKE node pool with partition 1g.5gb, which means one compute unit — 1/7 of the streaming multiprocessors — and 5 GB of memory, letting up to seven pods share one GPU so the stuck second model finally ran, while warning that sizing is dark magic best settled in the documentation, not by intuition [zuRKdveFuZ4 @ 00:10:19]. SUSE pushes MIG into VMs on Harvester 170: a MIG configurations CRD is auto-created by querying the driver, three profiles (1G.5GB, 2G.10GB, 3G.20GB) are defined, and each vGPU partition attaches to a VM [4q3LHacRheg @ 00:00:48]. Emmanuel Corels Academy lists the raw commands, nvidia-smi -l and nvidia-smi mig -l gip, and warns workloads need both GPU and compute instances, with some models requiring a reset [sRtvITK_o8I @ 00:01:38].

Fractional sharing with real memory enforcement is where the numbers get precise. Saiyam's KAI pattern is to annotate gpu-fraction 0.5 while keeping the resource limit at 1 [sXpJ4vSc-cM @ 00:38:38]. Julien Semaan of Kubex runs three workloads with gpu-fraction annotations of 0.35, 0.20 and 0.35 plus a reservation pod, but stresses KAI controls placement only; the fix is HAMi-core, which intercepts CUDA calls via LD_PRELOAD and converts a 0.35 fraction into an 8,061 MB CUDA_DEVICE_MEMORY_LIMIT, after which only the leaky classifier OOMs instead of the LLM beside it [Vw7DTM1SV60 @ 00:14:00]. The Code Architect applies the same discipline to Ray: a 0.25 GPU request only sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, so vLLM's GPU memory utilization must be tuned to match the Ray placement fraction [TwICQ_zP8Ys @ 00:07:14]. Yuan Chen's benchmarks put MPS limits in hard figures: under heavy inference load, capping a low-priority job at 10 percent gives the high-priority job near-dedicated performance, and on GPU burn, where one job consumes about 23 to 24 GB and time slicing let job 1 take roughly 10 times job 2's memory, MPS with 50 percent limits fixed the imbalance, while the MPS daemon itself costs about 20 MB [nOgxv_R13Dg @ 00:20:02].

callout.title: Settings that separate working shared clusters from OOM cascades
callout.body: Four field-tested adjustments the practitioners applied once the basic operator install was running.
items: Match vLLM's GPU memory utilization to the Ray placement fraction, because a 0.25 GPU request on its own can still saturate 100 percent of the device and let PyTorch and vLLM each grab the whole VRAM [The Code Architect — TwICQ_zP8Ys @ 00:07:14].
Do not trust nvidia-smi on time-sliced cards: on a 24 GB L4 with 5 replicas it showed 13 GB while the pod's real usage was 4 GB [CNCF — Vw7DTM1SV60 @ 00:04:56].

Inside each tenant vCluster, reinstall the GPU operator with the toolkit and driver disabled, reapply and re-patch time slicing, and refresh the node if the 4 replicas do not show [vCluster — KzJvhbdgvl8 @ 00:02:09].

Set NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES to compute and utility when the model does not use video, keep the nvidia.com/gpu limit explicit, and add a toleration keyed nvidia.com/gpu to clear the GPU node's NoSchedule taint [DevOps & AI Toolkit — zuRKdveFuZ4 @ 00:07:02].

sop_steps.title: Install and verify the GPU operator
sop_steps.action: Add the nvidia Helm repo, install gpu-operator with a values.yml setting the containerd template, socket path and nvidia runtime class, then run a test pod.
sop_steps.detail: Run helm repo add nvidia and helm repo update, install into the gpu-operator namespace with --create-namespace --wait, confirm the driver daemonset, device plugin, DCGM exporter and toolkit pods come up after a couple more minutes, then kubectl exec a GPU count 1 TensorFlow pod and run nvidia-smi [Techi Nik — f-FKoMHqRoI @ 00:04:27].

sop_steps.title: Apply the sharing profile by label
sop_steps.action: Pick time-slice replicas or a MIG layout and drive it through the node label that the operator watches.
sop_steps.detail: For time slicing, edit the node's nvidia.com label to a blueprint profile such as six or ten and let the operator reconcile the advertised GPU count in seconds; for MIG, let the GPU Operator's MIG manager apply a named configuration set through a node label [Rafay Systems — n-O8p7y9Z5A @ 00:01:29].

sop_steps.title: Enforce per-tenant memory at runtime
sop_steps.action: Pair fractional placement with a runtime memory cap so one tenant cannot OOM the card.
sop_steps.detail: Annotate pods with KAI gpu-fraction values such as 0.35 and 0.20 for placement, then inject HAMi-core so the 0.35 fraction becomes an 8,061 MB CUDA_DEVICE_MEMORY_LIMIT via LD_PRELOAD and only the misbehaving pod OOMs [CNCF — Vw7DTM1SV60 @ 00:14:00].

sop_steps.title: Benchmark shared versus isolated and rebalance
sop_steps.action: Run identical jobs shared and on separate instances, ramp concurrency, and adjust layouts on a fixed cadence.
sop_steps.detail: Give each job a distinct CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, measure latency and throughput while ramping users, and remember nvidia-smi does not attribute utilization per instance, which is how an A100 at 50 users showed 0.76 versus 1.0 requests/s per GPU [Emmanuel Corels Academy — sRtvITK_o8I @ 00:02:25].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is the classic one, time slicing versus MIG, and the practitioners do not land in the same place. Emmanuel Corels Academy ran the same jobs shared and then on separate MIG instances on an A100, with a distinct CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES per job, and at 50 users throughput moved from 0.76 to 1.0 requests per second per GPU, yet mean speech latency came in lower with time sharing [sRtvITK_o8I @ 00:03:35]. So the answer depends on whether a tenant is buying throughput or responsiveness. Julien Semaan of Kubex concedes in Q&A that MIG is usually faster but static, and his entire build targets making time slicing memory-safe rather than abandoning it [Vw7DTM1SV60 @ 00:20:40]. Kevin Klues frames it as a fundamental inherent trade-off: MIG buys full fault isolation and memory-bandwidth QoS but locks you into fixed partition sizes, while time partitioning gives flexibility that you pay for in contention [nOgxv_R13Dg @ 00:05:00]. The Code Architect settles the fight by workload class instead of ideology: time slicing for bursty heterogeneous workloads, MPS for trusted and predictable ones, and MIG only when you need absolute isolation [TwICQ_zP8Ys @ 00:08:03]. The operator read is that no single sharing mode wins every tenant mix, so each tenant gets placed and priced by the load profile it actually runs, not by whichever mode the platform team installed first.

Fractional GPUs split the field a second time, over whether a fraction is a promise or an enforced wall. Saiyam and Mike Peterson at vCluster demo the KAI approach: annotate the pod with gpu-fraction 0.5 while keeping the limit at 1 [sXpJ4vSc-cM @ 00:38:38]. Semaan warns that this controls placement only; KAI does not enforce the fraction at runtime, so noisy neighbors remain possible, and his fix layers HAMi-core underneath, intercepting CUDA calls through LD_PRELOAD so a 0.35 fraction becomes an 8,061 MB CUDA_DEVICE_MEMORY_LIMIT [Vw7DTM1SV60 @ 00:10:30]. The Code Architect hits the same wall from the Ray side: a 0.25 GPU request can still saturate the whole device because Ray only sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, so the fix lives in the application, tuning vLLM's GPU memory utilization to match the Ray placement fraction [TwICQ_zP8Ys @ 00:06:22]. Yuan Chen's benchmarks push a third playbook, MPS with explicit limits: capping a low-priority job at 10% gave the other job near-dedicated performance under heavy load, where plain time slicing pinned the GPU at 100% and degraded badly [nOgxv_R13Dg @ 00:20:45]. Semaan's own talk counters that MPS adds a daemon that becomes another point of failure. The real choice is where enforcement lives: in the CUDA interception layer, in each application's memory config, or in an extra daemon on every GPU node.

The tenancy wrapper is the third fault line. vCluster's Saiyam and Mike Peterson argue namespaces provide weak isolation, you can't do CRDs, and 3,000 secrets in one namespace load etcd for everyone, so each tenant gets its own virtual cluster, with the host either syncing node information in or exposing only a runtime class [sXpJ4vSc-cM @ 00:41:50]. Core Concept Learning's Run:ai playbook stays in one shared cluster and runs it like a quota market: departments and projects hold guaranteed GPU quotas, research borrows analytics' idle GPUs overnight, and preemption claws the quota back when the owner returns [56JbSXiXhhE @ 00:00:56]. Luca Berton's OpenShift AI build for a French avionics customer is governance-heavy: tenants arrive through PR-based templates covering RBAC, network policies and quotas, while KAI caps, priority classes and preemption keep interactive work above training [nABVTFBmV2M @ 00:13:02]. SUSE moves the boundary down to the virtual machine, carving MIG-backed vGPUs in Harvester into 1G.5GB, 2G.10GB and 3G.20GB profiles and attaching each partition to its own VM, with both VMs seeing the GPU [4q3LHacRheg @ 00:00:48]. Each camp trades operational weight for a harder boundary: borrowing is light and fast, PR-gated templates leave an audit trail, and VM-attached partitions give the hardest line of the four. The operator picks the wrapper first, then picks the slicing mode that runs underneath it.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Memory is where shared GPUs die first. Julien Semaan's Kubex demo put 5 time-slice replicas on a 24 GB L4, and nvidia-smi showed 13 GB for a pod whose real usage was 4 GB, so the standard tool misreported who was actually eating the card [Vw7DTM1SV60 @ 00:04:56]. Then a leaky classifier on the same GPU pushed LLM A into OOM, killing the well-behaved tenant instead of the offender. The Code Architect traces the same failure to layer misalignment: when hardware, driver and orchestration layers disagree, the result is OOM errors and node crashes, and Ray's fractional request only sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, letting PyTorch and vLLM each grab the whole VRAM [TwICQ_zP8Ys @ 00:01:14]. Yuan Chen's GPU-burn benchmark quantified the imbalance: under plain time slicing, job 1 took about ten times job 2's memory, and only MPS with 50% limits evened it out [nOgxv_R13Dg @ 00:23:49]. Dynamia.ai's HAMi talk adds the utilization cost: without memory isolation, OOM crashes tanked utilization, and reserved memory, 5 GB in their example, is not the same thing as consumed memory, so unused reservations and noisy neighbors both have to be watched [zrGFmLHI7hg @ 00:09:22]. The economics check is blunt: an unenforced fraction is an outage waiting for the noisiest neighbor on the card, and it takes down the paying tenant first.

The second trap is capacity that exists on paper but never schedules. Jitesh Powankar frames the baseline waste: a pod requesting a whole card may use only 20 to 30 percent, leaving 70 percent idle while other pods queue, like booking a whole 50-seat bus for one passenger [Ul1dZowvKvE @ 00:00:34]. DevOps & AI Toolkit hit it live on GKE: after llama 2 took the single GPU, the second model sat Pending with no available GPUs, and adding another node before the first was at full capacity would have been a waste of money; recreating the pool with 1g.5gb partitions let up to seven pods share the card [zuRKdveFuZ4 @ 00:08:47]. vCluster's host-cluster walkthrough showed the inverse problem: without time-slicing replicas advertised, pods simply fail to schedule, so the replica count has to be confirmed on the node before tenants arrive [KzJvhbdgvl8 @ 00:04:26]. Gang scheduling is the costliest version: with 8 pods and 4 GPUs, the default scheduler places 4 and leaves 4 pending, so the job never starts while 4 GPUs are still consumed [sXpJ4vSc-cM @ 00:37:13]. DevOps & AI Toolkit also flags the quieter blocker: GPU nodes carry a NoSchedule taint, so a pod without the nvidia.com/gpu toleration never lands on the hardware you are paying for.

The third failure class is drift, and it hits the teams that are already winning. Saiyam warns that deleting the GPU operator leaves drivers on the node, and a reinstall then produces a version mismatch that just breaks [sXpJ4vSc-cM @ 00:01:22]. Luca Berton's air-gapped H200 build lost time to a ConnectX versus Intel RDMA kernel collision that blocked SR-IOV until the Intel driver was blacklisted, and the team's upgrade path now runs through a compatibility matrix in Git, a 48-hour canary pool and Argo CD rollback [nABVTFBmV2M @ 00:11:34]. Dynamia.ai reports that NVIDIA GPU operator updates very often change or break metrics, so metric pipelines have to be re-verified after every operator bump [zrGFmLHI7hg @ 00:10:03]. Core Concept Learning names the policy traps directly: static per-team GPUs, a whole GPU for every notebook, changing the MIG layout while work is running, and preemption without checkpointing [56JbSXiXhhE @ 00:02:19]. The payoff for avoiding them is real, with overall GPU utilization roughly doubling after a month of quota rebalancing, a MIG relayout on two drained nodes and coaching for idle-notebook users. Christian Kniep's checkpoint operator closes the preemption gap by restoring a PyTorch job at epoch 4 after the pod is deleted, for jobs carrying the checkpoint labels.

callout.title: Do not open a shared GPU to a second tenant until these four checks pass
callout.body: Every item below comes from a practitioner who lost a model, a job or a dashboard to it. Clear all four before advertising slices, fractions or borrowing to another team.
items: Memory is enforced at runtime, not only annotated: KAI placement alone leaves noisy neighbors possible, so wrap fractions in a CUDA-level memory limit [CNCF — Vw7DTM1SV60 @ 00:10:30].
MIG layouts are only changed on drained nodes; changing the layout while work is running is a named trap [Core Concept Learning — 56JbSXiXhhE @ 00:02:19].
Preemptible jobs checkpoint to a PVC first, so a reclaimed pod resumes at the next epoch instead of restarting from zero [Christian Kniep — K9yY6_2255Y @ 00:02:24].
GPU operator upgrades are canaried with metrics re-verified, because operator updates very often change or break metrics [CNCF — zrGFmLHI7hg @ 00:10:03].

chapters.pull_quote: "When we do time slicing on Kubernetes, we're basically tricking the scheduler into thinking there are more GPUs available for scheduling than there are physically." Julien Semaan, Kubex, attributed to CNCF [Cloud Native Computing Foundation] (Vw7DTM1SV60 @ 00:06:57).
action_checklist: Install the GPU operator with helm install gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator -n gpu-operator --create-namespace --wait -f values.yml, with the Nvidia runtime set as default, then confirm the driver, device plugin, DCGM exporter and toolkit pods [Techi Nik — f-FKoMHqRoI @ 00:03:20].

Drive time-slice replica counts from a node label backed by blueprint profiles for 2, 6 and 10 replicas, and confirm the advertised GPU count flips within seconds [Rafay Systems — n-O8p7y9Z5A @ 00:02:13].
For MIG single strategy on an A100, deploy a test app and verify all pods share one GPU UUID with distinct MIG UUIDs before onboarding tenants [Rafay Systems — YoZoDn_Fvq0 @ 00:02:55].
Back every fractional request with HAMi-core so the fraction converts into a hard CUDA_DEVICE_MEMORY_LIMIT and only the leaking workload OOMs [CNCF — Vw7DTM1SV60 @ 00:14:00].
Set guaranteed project quotas, allow over-quota borrowing of idle GPUs, and require regular checkpointing so preempted work resumes cleanly [Core Concept Learning — 56JbSXiXhhE @ 00:00:56].
Track per-slice memory and compute in Prometheus and Grafana with alerts, then rebalance slice counts as usage shifts between light and heavy tenants [Jitesh Powankar — Ul1dZowvKvE @ 00:04:15].

chapters.question_prompt: Which inference engine and settings squeeze the most tokens per GPU dollar out of the hardware I have?
chapters.title: Inference Engines: Getting Maximum Tokens per GPU
chapters.subtitle: vLLM PagedAttention and its three memory settings, SGLang RadixAttention, TGI, KV cache and FlashAttention, continuous batching, quantization, memory bandwidth vs FLOPS, a token's journey through vLLM and SGLang, Crusoe managed inference, and llama.cpp vs vLLM vs SGLang benchmarks on one GPU
chapters.executive_summary: Operators tuning inference engines agree that decode is memory-bound: every token streams every weight, so tokens per GPU come from packing more concurrent sequences behind each weight read. PagedAttention and continuous batching are the baseline; KodeKloud lifted KV utilization from about 20% to roughly 95% with 16-token pages, and DataMListic credits continuous batching with an order of magnitude in throughput. The street mechanics are a handful of knobs: max-model-len, max-num-batched-tokens, max-num-seqs, KV pool fraction, FP8 or 4-bit quantization, and chunked prefill budgets that trade time to first token against inter-token latency. The split is engine choice: vLLM for independent requests, dense models, and very large clusters; SGLang once shared-prefix tokens pass 40%, with 2 times or more throughput above 70%. Benchmarks conflict, with Lukasz Gawenda measuring vLLM ahead on TTFT and end-to-end latency while SGLang won TPOT.

key_metrics.context: Hands-on vLLM lab where a 512-token reservation wasted roughly 80% of KV memory until page size 16 was applied

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator here starts from the same physics: decode is starved by memory, not math. DataMListic lays it out bluntly: each generated token requires reading every weight, so a 70B model streams roughly 140 GB per token while the compute units mostly sit and wait, and batching four requests means one weight load yields four tokens: “Same cost, four times the throughput” [X8CwAqYxH1E @ 00:00:41]. AI WITH Rithesh puts hard numbers on an H100: 80 GB of HBM at 3.35 TB/s against 989 TFLOPS works out to about 295 ops per byte, and on a 27B model the compute takes 55 microseconds versus 16 ms of memory reads, capping single-user decode near 60 tok/s: “The memory side takes almost 300 times longer” [lasG5MsR-gE @ 00:07:36]. Micro Learning frames the same split as two phases, with prefill compute-bound and decode memory-bound [zkMCHA5uzIo @ 00:01:18]. Serverside Acquisitions takes it to the hardware-spend level, claiming $400B went into chips that sit 85% idle because each token hauls every parameter through the chip, the math finishes in under a microsecond, and the $40,000 accelerator then idles [BFMPHZZBGlg @ 00:00:00]. The operator takeaway is unanimous: tokens per GPU is won by keeping weights streaming to as many concurrent sequences as possible.

The second point of agreement is that legacy serving burns most of its KV memory, and paging fixes it. KodeKloud states traditional systems waste 60 to 80% of KV memory, and in their lab a 512-token reservation hit only about 20% utilization before PagedAttention with page size 16 pushed it to roughly 95%, supporting 4 to 5 times more users [qdPkA5mxLhg @ 00:08:00]. Neural AI Flair gives the arithmetic: 4K tokens eat more than 1 GB per request on an A100-80GB, generating 300 of a possible 2,000 tokens wastes 84%, and 16-token pages cut fragmentation below 4% [18AkpuX3vkY @ 00:01:19]. On scheduling, DataMListic shows static batching leaving 14 of 32 slots producing nothing, keeping the GPU busy “barely more than half the time,” while continuous batching evicts finished rows each step, keeps the card “essentially full,” and is worth “an order of magnitude in throughput” [X8CwAqYxH1E @ 00:03:23]. Uplatz adds the cost of ignoring this: static batching reserves for the worst case, so a GPU can throw out-of-memory errors while functionally idle, and Ollama, with no continuous batching, is prototype-only [jp2pwEpUg-Q @ 00:00:17]. Every practitioner treats paging plus continuous batching as the non-negotiable baseline for tokens per GPU, not an optional upgrade.

Practitioners also converge on who the contenders are and roughly where each fits, even while they argue over the margins. Vizuara claims private open-source LLM deployments “almost always” run on vLLM or SGLang, and frames the payoff as cutting a $2M-per-year deployment to $200K [f4WDLg2sbx4 @ 00:01:59]. Crusoe AI's solutions engineer Martin Calla says both engines are built on paged attention, calls vLLM the “veteran” throughput default for dense models like Llama, and positions SGLang for MoE models such as DeepSeek and Qwen plus function calling and JSON: “If you just need raw inference, speed and reliability, vLLM is the stable option” [R74kx7GKEbs @ 00:02:10]. System Decisions lands in the same place, noting both engines come out of UC Berkeley, with vLLM winning single-turn and batch work and SGLang built around radix-tree prefix reuse and compressed FSMs for conversational, structured, or agentic traffic [KSQQ4-K5eW0 @ 00:05:30]. Tensor Garage compresses it into a single rule of thumb from single-GPU testing on an RTX 4090: “llama.cpp to fit and interact, vLLM to batch… SGLang to reuse” [Ym3TP9rlzCk @ 00:12:15]. The shared prerequisite is a real serving engine with paging and continuous batching underneath; none of these operators recommends pushing concurrent production traffic through a prototype runtime.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: On vLLM, the tuning surface is small and brutal. Lukasz Gawenda isolates three settings that decide throughput and latency: max-model-len (16K in their walkthrough, where a 10K-token request passes and an 18K one is rejected), max-num-batched-tokens (12K), and max-num-seqs; chunked prefill, the V1 default, splits a 30K request into 8 chunks while prioritizing decodes, and a smaller token budget buys better inter-token latency while a larger one buys better time to first token [ycEQJIyZ2sU @ 00:09:44]. Vizuara traces the same budget inside the engine: a 2,048-token step cap filled with 127 decode tokens plus 1,921 prefill tokens, with the remaining 79 pushed to step N+1 and the next-token prediction from the partial prefill discarded [IDjyrXKsC5U @ 00:37:00]. AI WITH Rithesh shows why the memory fraction matters: vLLM claims 90% of the H100, leaving about 18 GB of KV cache on their 27B example, which fills at roughly 28 users holding 8K tokens each [lasG5MsR-gE @ 00:10:06]. KodeKloud runs the opposite extreme on a tiny SmolLM-135M lab, dropping max-model-len to 64 and max-num-seqs to 8, serving on localhost:8000/v1 with the API key literally “not needed,” and watching throughput climb with only a slight latency rise as load steps from 1 to 5 to 10 to 20 users [qdPkA5mxLhg @ 00:11:33].

SGLang's edge is prefix reuse, and the practitioners who run it put hard numbers on exactly how much shared context it takes to pay off. Neural AI Flair reports radix cache hit rates of 60 to 90%, and a shared-token rule: below 20% shared tokens the engines are equal, above 40% SGLang wins, and “Above 70%, expect two times or more throughput on the same hardware”; they also report TTFT up to 5 times lower for SGLang with equal time between tokens [18AkpuX3vkY @ 00:06:19]. Vizuara explains why vLLM can only reuse true prefixes: blocks hold 16 tokens and each block hash chains to the previous one, so arbitrary substrings never match, while SGLang runs a token-level radix tree with LRU eviction and schedules requests with the most cached tokens first; semantic similarity does not count, because keys and values depend on position embedding [IDjyrXKsC5U @ 00:48:44]. AI WITH Rithesh adds that SGLang's router lifts cache hit rate from 20% to 75% and throughput up to 1.9 times, with grammar-forced multi-token output for structured responses [lasG5MsR-gE @ 00:18:11]. Micro Learning warns that prompt caching needs an exact prefix match and expires on a TTL, so any change at the front of a prompt kills the hit [zkMCHA5uzIo @ 00:03:31].

Quantization is the most direct multiplier the practitioners quote. AI WITH Rithesh walks a 27B model from 54 GB in BF16 to 27 GB in FP8 to 14 GB at 4-bit, lifting single-stream throughput from about 60 to 120 to roughly 240 tok/s, notes Marlin W4A16 delivers around 4 times up to batch 16 to 32, and points out that an FP8 KV cache halves per-token cost to 32 KB; their vLLM recipe is TP=4, FP8 KV cache, and 3 draft tokens [lasG5MsR-gE @ 00:11:12]. Lukasz Gawenda, squeezing a 176B-parameter model onto one 96 GB card, set SGLang's KV pool fraction to 0.9 and got only 166k tokens, found raising it cost 1.3 GB, and advises setting it lower because GUI VRAM use varies between restarts, running at concurrency 1 to 2 [RlsxXB5q-cA @ 00:32:34]. For measurement, Tensor Garage fixes model, tokenizer, quantization, lengths, and concurrency, keeps streaming on, warms up, clears the prefix cache, and records median and p99 latency for TPOT and goodput [Ym3TP9rlzCk @ 00:00:49]. Gawenda's head-to-head used bench_serving on ShareGPT with 1,000 prompts at full burst and 10 warm-ups on an L40S-48C vGPU with 14 vCPUs serving a Qwen Coder FP8 model [gkl2KlJ7FP0 @ 00:12:39].

callout.title: How the benchmarkers actually work the engines
callout.body: Small habits the hands-on operators use to get clean numbers and visible bottlenecks before committing GPU spend.
items: Benchmark with everything pinned: fix model, tokenizer, quantization, lengths, and concurrency, keep streaming on, warm up, clear the prefix cache, and record median and p99 [Tensor Garage — Ym3TP9rlzCk @ 00:00:49].
Run your own accuracy checks because official benchmarks are leaked; a McNemar test at the p<0.05 threshold found no GGUF vs NVFP4 difference [Lukasz Gawenda — RlsxXB5q-cA @ 00:34:02].
Before tuning, feed the vLLM repo into NotebookLM to get through the internals fast [Lukasz Gawenda — gkl2KlJ7FP0 @ 00:11:24].
Wire Prometheus and Grafana onto the vLLM server so throughput and latency are visible as user counts climb [KodeKloud — qdPkA5mxLhg @ 00:13:06].

sop_steps.title: Size the KV budget before anything else
sop_steps.action: Subtract model weights and a safety buffer from VRAM to get the KV pool you can distribute across users.
sop_steps.detail: Vizuara's worked example: Llama 3.1 8B in BF16 takes 16 GB on an 80 GB H100, a 10 GB buffer is held back, and 54 GB remains for KV cache across users sending 2,000 tokens each [Vizuara — IDjyrXKsC5U @ 00:12:09].

sop_steps.title: Install and expose an OpenAI-compatible endpoint
sop_steps.action: pip install vLLM on a Linux VM or Kubernetes and serve the model through the OpenAI-compatible API.
sop_steps.detail: IBM Technology's workflow is pip install on a Linux VM or Kubernetes, then serve through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with vLLM optimized for quantized models [IBM Technology — McLdlg5Gc9s @ 00:03:58].

sop_steps.title: Set the three throughput and latency knobs
sop_steps.action: Configure max-model-len, max-num-batched-tokens, and max-num-seqs, then tune the chunked prefill budget.
sop_steps.detail: Gawenda's settings were max-model-len 16K and max-num-batched-tokens 12K; shrink the budget for better inter-token latency, grow it for better time to first token [Lukasz Gawenda — ycEQJIyZ2sU @ 00:00:00].

sop_steps.title: Load test, then route by shared-prefix ratio
sop_steps.action: Burst-test with real-shaped prompts, then move shared-prefix traffic to SGLang once overlap is high enough.
sop_steps.detail: Run bench_serving on ShareGPT with 1,000 prompts at full burst and 10 warm-ups [Lukasz Gawenda — gkl2KlJ7FP0 @ 00:12:39]; switch to SGLang above 40% shared tokens and expect 2 times or more above 70% [Neural AI Flair — 18AkpuX3vkY @ 00:06:19].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The head-to-head numbers do not line up, and operators should treat each benchmark as a workload fingerprint rather than a verdict. Lukasz Gawenda ran bench_serving on ShareGPT with 1,000 prompts at full burst on an L40S vGPU with a Qwen Coder FP8 model, and vLLM took the headline: lower total duration, end-to-end latency of 220 seconds against 355, and time to first token of 138 against 285 [gkl2KlJ7FP0 @ 00:20:38]. SGLang still won the per-token race in that same run, posting 1.45 times better TPOT and smoother inter-token latency [gkl2KlJ7FP0 @ 00:21:56]. Neural AI Flair reports the opposite on the first-token axis, crediting SGLang with up to 5 times lower TTFT while calling time between tokens equal [18AkpuX3vkY @ 00:07:00]. Tensor Garage adds a third reading from published results: SGLang cut TTFT by 30 to 58 percent across seven MoE models on an H200, while vLLM held an 18 percent decode edge [Ym3TP9rlzCk @ 00:01:46]. The street lesson is that first-token speed, steady decode and total batch duration can each crown a different engine on the same day, so the metric that actually pays your bills decides the winner, not the reputation of the repo or the star count on its page.

Where practitioners do converge is on letting the shape of the traffic pick the engine, but they draw the dividing line in different places. Neural AI Flair puts a number on it: general throughput on Llama 3 70B lands at 17,000 to 19,000 tokens per second with both engines within 15 percent of each other, shared tokens below 20 percent make them equal, above 40 percent SGLang wins, and above 70 percent the operator should expect two times or more throughput on the same hardware [18AkpuX3vkY @ 00:06:19]. System Decisions draws the line by job type instead, routing stable or single-round work to vLLM and conversational, structured or agentic work to SGLang, while conceding vLLM can be faster on a single long generation [KSQQ4-K5eW0 @ 00:05:30]. Crusoe AI solutions engineer Martin Calla splits by model architecture, calling vLLM the veteran throughput default for dense models like Llama and pointing SGLang at MoE models such as DeepSeek and Qwen, plus function calling and JSON output [R74kx7GKEbs @ 00:02:28]. Vizuara adds a hardware axis: heavy prefix sharing on Nvidia or AMD goes to SGLang, other chips go to vLLM, and everything else gets measured before anyone commits capacity [IDjyrXKsC5U @ 01:22:26].

A second camp argues the two-horse race is the wrong frame entirely. Uplatz lays out a decision map that pushes sub-100 millisecond latency to TensorRT-LLM, 100,000-token documents or AMD and Intel hardware to TGI, and concurrent chat to vLLM, backing the TGI call with a claim that TGI v3 processes 200,000-token prompts up to 13 times faster than vLLM while giving up chat throughput; the same channel dismisses Ollama as prototype-only because it lacks continuous batching [jp2pwEpUg-Q @ 00:05:11]. Tensor Garage compresses its single-GPU verdict into one rule: llama.cpp to fit and interact, vLLM to batch, SGLang to reuse [Ym3TP9rlzCk @ 00:12:15]. KodeKloud keeps llama.cpp in the kit specifically for CPU and RAM-only inference where no GPU is available [qdPkA5mxLhg @ 00:13:23]. Lukasz Gawenda's oversized Qwen3.8 Flash test adds a fourth option and makes the choice before any number is measured: if weights fit in VRAM, run SGLang or vLLM for better long context and day-one speculative decoding; if you want to name every memory destination yourself, run llama.cpp on the widest hardware range; if you would rather not tune at all, FreeToken sizes itself [RlsxXB5q-cA @ 00:24:56].
